stem: 25 yrs old male, non-visible haematuria, father and brother had similar asymptomatic non-visible haematuria. Urinalysis: Blood 4+ Protein negative No casts Creatinine: deranged What is the most likely cause of the presentation?
explanation:
Correct Answer

A. Alport syndrome

Key Points from the Scenario

•

25-year-old male → young adult presentation.

•

Asymptomatic non-visible haematuria → chronic glomerular disease is
likely.

Family history (father & brother with same finding) → hereditary

cause strongly suggested.

•

Urinalysis: Blood 4+, protein negative, no casts → isolated haematuria

without proteinuria or nephritic sediment → glomerular structural
problem.

•

Creatinine deranged → progressive renal dysfunction.

MRCP Syndrome Key Clue = hereditary haematuria + progressive renal

impairment.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Alport Syndrome)

•

Alport syndrome is a hereditary nephritis due to mutations in type IV

collagen (α5 chain, COL4A5 gene).

•

Most commonly X-linked, but can also be autosomal recessive or dominant.

•

Features:

o

Asymptomatic microscopic haematuria (often in childhood or young

adulthood).

o

Progressive renal impairment leading to CKD/ESKD.

o

Family history in males (X-linked).

o

Hearing loss (sensorineural deafness) and ocular abnormalities may

develop.

•

Fits this case: young male + family history + non-visible haematuria +

rising creatinine.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Exercise-induced haematuria

o

Transient, occurs after strenuous activity.

o

Self-limiting, no family history, no renal impairment.

o

Does not fit this chronic, familial pattern.

IgA nephropathy

o

Most common glomerulonephritis worldwide.

o

Presents with recurrent visible haematuria,

often post-URTI

("synpharyngitic").

o

Family history not typical, and proteinuria often present later.

Thin basement membrane disease

o

Also, familial and presents with isolated microscopic haematuria.

o

BUT → normal renal function and benign course (no progression to

CKD).

o

Our case has deranged creatinine, so not just TBM disease.

Urothelial tumour

o

Typically, in older patients (\>50 years), risk

factors (smoking,

occupational exposure).

o

Causes painless visible haematuria.

o

Not consistent with family history or age.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Alport syndrome: young male, hereditary, haematuria, progressive renal

failure, hearing/ocular problems.

•

Thin basement membrane disease: benign familial haematuria, no

progression.

•

IgA nephropathy: synpharyngitic haematuria, variable progression.

•

Exercise haematuria: transient, benign.

•

Urothelial cancer: older patients, visible haematuria, not familial.

ALTERNATIVE SCENARIO

25 yrs old male, non-visible haematuria, father and brother had
similar asymptomatic

non-visible haematuria.

Urinalysis: Blood 4+

Protein negative

No casts

Creatinine: normal

What is the most likely cause of the presentation?

A. Alport syndrome

B. Exercise induced haematuria

C. IgA nephropathy

D. Thin basement membrane disease

E. Urothelial tumour

ANSWERS:

Thin basement membrane disease

Correct Answer

D. Thin basement membrane disease

Key Points from the Scenario

•

25-year-old male → young, otherwise healthy.

•

Asymptomatic non-visible haematuria → suggests a benign or inherited

cause.

•

Family history (father & brother with the same) → strong pointer toward
a

hereditary condition.

•

Urinalysis: Blood 4+, protein negative, no casts → isolated haematuria

without nephritic or nephrotic features.

•

Creatinine: normal → preserved renal function (rules against progressive

nephropathies like Alport).

MRCP Syndrome key clue = familial microscopic haematuria with normal
renal

function and no proteinuria → Thin Basement Membrane disease (benign
familial

haematuria).

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Thin Basement Membrane
Disease)

•

Also called benign familial haematuria.

•

Caused by defect in type IV collagen affecting the glomerular basement

membrane, but in a milder form than Alport syndrome.

•

Features:

o

Lifelong microscopic haematuria.

o

Family history often positive.

o

Normal renal function and no progression to CKD (distinguishes from

Alport).

No extrarenal features (hearing loss/ocular problems absent).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Alport syndrome

o

Also, familial haematuria, but associated with progressive renal

impairment, proteinuria, and sensorineural deafness/ocular defects.

o

Our patient's creatinine is normal, and no mention of deafness.

Exercise-induced haematuria

o

Transient, occurs after strenuous activity, resolves spontaneously.

o

No family history, not persistent.

IgA nephropathy

o

Causes recurrent haematuria, often macroscopic following

infections ("synpharyngitic").

o

Can cause proteinuria and progressive renal disease.

o

Not purely familial isolated microscopic haematuria.

Thin basement membrane disease

o

Perfect fit: familial, asymptomatic, isolated

haematuria, normal renal

function.

Urothelial tumour

o

Typically, in older patients (\>50), presents with visible haematuria.

o

Not familial, not microscopic only.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Isolated haematuria + family history + normal creatinine → Thin
basement

membrane disease.

•

Haematuria + family history + progressive renal failure/deafness →
Alport

syndrome.

•

Haematuria following infections → IgA

nephropathy.

•

Older patient with visible haematuria → Urothelial carcinoma.

stem: A 50 year Patient presents with breathlessness, underwent lung transplant 4 yrs back for lung fibrosis, 2 yrs before transplant stopped smoking, patient is on co- trimoxazole. PFT - Airflow obstruction Diagnosis?
explanation:
Bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome (BOS)

Key Points from the Scenario

•

50-year-old, 4 years post--lung transplant for pulmonary fibrosis.

•

On co-trimoxazole prophylaxis → rules out Pneumocystis jirovecii
pneumonia.

•

PFT: airflow obstruction (↓FEV1, ↓FEV1/FVC).

•

Chronic transplant complication rather than infection or recurrence.

Detailed Explanation

•

Bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome = manifestation of chronic lung
allograft

dysfunction (CLAD).

•

Pathophysiology: immune-mediated injury → small airway fibrosis →

progressive obstructive pattern.

•

Usually develops \>3 months after transplant, often several years later.

•

Clinical: progressive breathlessness, cough, wheeze.

•

PFT hallmark: airflow obstruction (↓FEV1).

•

It is the most common cause of late allograft failure after lung

transplantation.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

B. COPD → He quit smoking before transplant; and post-transplant COPD

recurrence is not the issue. Obstruction here is due to chronic
rejection.

•

C. P. jiroveci pneumonia → Prevented by co-trimoxazole; would present
with

acute infection + ground-glass changes, not chronic obstruction.

•

D. Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) → Causes mass

lesions, systemic illness, lymphadenopathy; not obstructive PFT.

•

E. Recurrent fibrosis → Fibrosis recurrence (e.g., IPF) is rare
post-transplant,

and would show restrictive PFT, not obstructive.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Early complication post-lung transplant = infection, acute rejection.

•

Late complication = BOS (chronic rejection, obstructive PFT).

•

Obstructive PFT post--lung transplant = Bronchiolitis obliterans syndrom

Lung Transplant Complications

Timing Complication Key Features Exam Clue

Early (\<3 months)

Infection (bacterial, viral, fungal,

PCP)

Fever, cough, infiltrates,

hypoxia

Immunosuppressed, co-trimoxazole

prevents PCP

Primary graft dysfunction ARDS-like picture within 72h Hypoxia +
bilateral infiltrates

Acute rejection

Dyspnoea, cough, ↓O₂, patchy

infiltrates

Lymphocytic infiltration on biopsy

Anastomotic complications Stricture, dehiscence, stenosis Wheeze,
localized obstruction

Late (\>3 months --

years)

Bronchiolitis obliterans

syndrome (BOS)

Progressive airflow

obstruction, ↓FEV1

Most common cause of chronic

rejection

Recurrent disease (rare: e.g.,

sarcoidosis, IPF, CF)

Depends on original pathology Pattern matches original ILD/CF

Malignancy (skin cancers, solid

organ)

Immunosuppression risk SCC of skin most common

Post-transplant

lymphoproliferative disorder

(PTLD)

EBV-driven lymphoma,

lymphadenopathy, fever,

weight loss

Mass lesions on imaging

Infection (chronic

opportunistic)

CMV, fungal, TB

Reactivation in long-term

immunosuppression

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Airflow obstruction (obstructive PFT) = BOS (chronic rejection).

•

Restrictive pattern = recurrence of underlying ILD (rare).

•

PCP prophylaxis = co-trimoxazole.

•

PTLD = EBV-driven, late complication, systemic lymphoma-like.

Mnemonic: "In ARB's Lungs" (for lung transplant complications)

•

Infection (early & late)

•

Acute rejection (early)

•

Recurrence of disease (late, rare)

•

Bronchiolitis obliterans (late, obstructive PFT)

•

Lymphoproliferative disorder & malignancy (late)

stem: A 45 y/o woman presents with worsening SOB, tired for 4 months. Complaints of tingling and numbness for 2 months. Hb 8.6, MCV high. Explanation?
explanation:
Correct Answer

A. Pernicious Anaemia

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Middle-aged woman (45 y/o).

•

Symptoms:

o

4 months of progressive SOB + fatigue (anaemia).

o

2 months of tingling & numbness (neuropathy).

•

Lab: Hb 8.6 g/dL, high MCV → macrocytic anaemia.

•

Classic for Vitamin B12 deficiency due to pernicious anaemia (autoimmune

gastritis with intrinsic factor antibodies).

Detailed Explanation (Pernicious Anaemia)

•

Macrocytic anaemia = high MCV.

•

Neurological features (tingling, numbness, neuropathy, subacute combined

degeneration) → specific for B12 deficiency, not folate.

•

Pernicious anaemia is the most common cause of B12 deficiency in

developed countries.

•

Autoimmune condition; associated with other autoimmune diseases
(thyroid,

vitiligo).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

B. Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA) → Anaemia, but usually

normocytic with jaundice, reticulocytosis, splenomegaly. No neuropathy.

•

C. Hypothyroidism → Can cause macrocytosis but not usually severe
anaemia

with neurological symptoms.

•

D. Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) → Causes macrocytosis and anaemia,

but neurological symptoms are not typical.

•

E. Thiamine deficiency → Causes beriberi/Wernicke's, not macrocytic
anaemia.

Macrocytic anaemia + neuropathy = B12 deficiency (most often Pernicious

Anaemia).

•

Macrocytic anaemia without neuropathy = Folate deficiency.

B12 vs Folate Deficiency

Feature Vitamin B12 Deficiency Folate Deficiency

Common Causes

Pernicious anaemia (IF Ab), gastrectomy,

Crohn's/ileal resection, vegan diet

Poor diet, alcoholism, pregnancy,

methotrexate, phenytoin

Onset Insidious (months--years, due to liver stores) Rapid
(weeks--months)

Anaemia Type Macrocytic, megaloblastic Macrocytic, megaloblastic

Neuro Symptoms

Yes → Peripheral neuropathy, subacute

combined degeneration (posterior + lateral

columns: ataxia, paraesthesia, spasticity)

Absent (no neurological involvement)

Other Clinical

Clues

Glossitis, lemon-tinted pallor, neuropsychiatric

changes

Glossitis, no neuro signs

Lab Findings

↑ MCV, hypersegmented neutrophils, low B12, ↑

homocysteine + ↑ methylmalonic acid

↑ MCV, hypersegmented neutrophils, low

folate, ↑ homocysteine (but normal

methylmalonic acid)

Special Tests

Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies, Schilling test

(historical)

Red cell folate assay

Treatment

IM hydroxocobalamin (lifelong if pernicious

anaemia)

Oral folate (but never before excluding

B12 deficiency, to avoid neuro damage)

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Neuropathy? → B12.

•

No neuropathy, rapid onset? → Folate.

•

Both → Macrocytic, megaloblastic anaemia.

•

Always check B12 before giving folate.

Mnemonic: "B12 = Brain, Folate = Food"

•

B12 → neurological (brain + cord).

•

Folate → dietary deficiency (alcohol, poor intake, pregnancy).

Macrocytic Anaemia: Diagnostic Algorithm

Step 1: Confirm Macrocytosis

•

MCV \> 100 fL → Macrocytic anaemia.

Step 2: Check if Megaloblastic (DNA synthesis defect)

Blood film / Bone marrow:

•

Hypersegmented neutrophils, oval macrocytes → Megaloblastic.

•

Round macrocytes, no hypersegmentation →

Non-megaloblastic.

Step 3A: Megaloblastic Causes

•

Vitamin B12 deficiency

o

Pernicious anaemia (anti-IF Ab)

o

Vegan diet, gastrectomy, ileal disease (Crohn's, resection)

o

Neuropathy, ↑ homocysteine, ↑ methylmalonic acid

•

Folate deficiency

o

Diet, alcoholism, pregnancy, drugs (MTX, phenytoin)

o

Glossitis, no neuro signs, ↑ homocysteine (normal methylmalonic acid)

Step 3B: Non-Megaloblastic Causes

•

Alcoholism → direct marrow toxicity, commonest cause.

•

Liver disease → altered lipid in RBC membrane.

•

Hypothyroidism → ↓ metabolism → macrocytosis.

•

Reticulocytosis (haemolysis, blood loss) → young large cells.

•

MDS (Myelodysplastic syndrome) → older patients, cytopenias, dysplastic

cells.

Step 4: Special Situations

•

Drug-induced → Hydroxyurea, AZT, chemotherapy.

•

Mixed deficiency (B12 + iron) → MCV may appear normal; look at RDW.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Neuro symptoms? → B12 deficiency.

•

Alcoholic with macrocytosis but no anaemia → think alcohol/liver.

•

Elderly with macrocytosis + cytopenias → MDS.

Never give folate before ruling out B12 deficiency.

Mnemonic for Macrocytosis: "Big Fat RBCs"

•

B12 / Folate deficiency

•

Inhibited DNA synthesis (MTX, chemo, AZT)

•

Gastro/liver disease

•

Failure of marrow (MDS)

•

Alcohol

•

Thyroid (hypo)

•

Reticulocytosis

•

Bone marrow disorders

•

Combination deficiencies

•

Splenectomy

stem: Person presented with right eye and neck pain. He had left sided tingling sensation 2 days back CT head - normal CTA - internal carotid artery thrombus just before bifurcation What cranial nerve abnormality can be seen here?
explanation:
Correct Answer

A. Left Horner syndrome

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Right eye + neck pain → suggests right internal carotid artery

dissection/thrombosis.

•

Left-sided tingling → contralateral hemisensory symptoms due to
ischaemia.

•

The internal carotid artery runs close to the sympathetic plexus that
supplies

the eye.

•

Dissection or thrombus can compress/disrupt these fibres → ipsilateral
Horner

syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Left 4th nerve palsy → Would cause vertical diplopia, but not related to

carotid thrombosis.

•

Left 3rd nerve palsy → Causes ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, dilated pupil ---
seen

in aneurysm/diabetes, not ICA dissection.

•

Left 6th nerve palsy → Lateral rectus palsy, often due to raised ICP,
not ICA

thrombus.

•

Right 6th nerve palsy → Same reasoning, not the typical feature of ICA

dissection.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Internal carotid artery dissection/thrombosis → classic triad:

Unilateral headache/neck/facial pain.

Partial Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis; anhidrosis may be absent).

Cerebral ischaemia (TIA/stroke symptoms --- contralateral weakness,

tingling).

Carotid vs Vertebral Artery Dissection

Feature Carotid Artery Dissection Vertebral Artery Dissection

Typical Pain

Unilateral head, face, or neck pain (often

periorbital or jaw)

Occipital headache, posterior neck pain

Local Signs

Partial Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, ±

anhidrosis) from sympathetic plexus

involvement

Usually no Horner's, but neck pain

prominent

Cranial Nerve

Involvement

CN IX--XII palsies (rare, due to mass effect) Lower cranial nerves less
involved

Stroke Pattern

Anterior circulation stroke/TIA

(contralateral weakness, numbness, aphasia if

dominant hemisphere)

Posterior circulation stroke/TIA (vertigo,

diplopia, ataxia, dysarthria, visual field

defects)

Ischaemic Symptoms

Hemiparesis, hemisensory loss, monocular

vision loss (amaurosis fugax)

Vertigo, imbalance, nystagmus, diplopia,

dysphagia

Risk Factors

Trauma (whiplash, chiropractic), connective

tissue disease (Marfan, Ehlers--Danlos),

hypertension

Same, plus sports/neck extension injuries

Imaging

CTA/MRA neck + head → tapering, "string

sign"

Same

Treatment Anticoagulation / antiplatelets Anticoagulation /
antiplatelets

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Carotid dissection = unilateral pain + Horner syndrome + anterior
circulation

stroke.

•

Vertebral dissection = posterior neck pain + posterior circulation
stroke

(vertigo, diplopia, ataxia).

Mnemonic:

•

"CARotid = CARdinal sign is Horner"

•

"VERTebral = VERTigo + posTERior circulation"

A 55 year female with bronchiectasis being treated with unable to
plantar flex and

presents with right heel pain.

Culprit drug?

Amoxicillin

Cefalexin

Clindamycin

Doxycycline

Levofloxacin

ANSWERS:

Levofloxacin

Correct Answer

Levofloxacin

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Bronchiectasis on treatment → requires recurrent antibiotics.

•

Now presents with right heel pain + unable to plantarflex → classic
for

Achilles tendinopathy/rupture.

•

Fluoroquinolones (e.g., levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin) are well known to
cause:

o

Tendonitis (especially Achilles)

o

Tendon rupture (risk ↑ with steroids, elderly, renal impairment).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Amoxicillin → Causes rash, allergy, diarrhoea; not tendinopathy.

•

Cefalexin → Beta-lactam antibiotic, no tendon effects.

•

Clindamycin → Causes diarrhoea, C. difficile colitis.

•

Doxycycline → Causes photosensitivity, oesophagitis; not tendon
rupture.

Fluoroquinolones → tendonitis & rupture (esp. Achilles).

•

Exam buzzword: "Heel pain + antibiotic = think fluoroquinolone."

stem: A 55 year old male, recent history of travel to Bolivia, presented with 3 days H/O increasing dizziness and lethargy. ECG: Bi-fascicular block and anterior Q waves Echocardiography: Poor LV Systolic Function + Dilated left ventricle Causative organisms?
explanation:
Correct Answer

E. Trypanosoma cruzi

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Travel to Bolivia → endemic area for Chagas disease.

•

Clinical findings:

o

Conduction defects (bi-fascicular block).

o

Anterior Q waves (prior infarction-like changes).

o

Poor LV function (cardiomyopathy).

•

This combination is highly suggestive of Chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy.

•

Causative organism: Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted by the reduviid

("kissing") bug.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

A. Borrelia burgdorferi → Lyme disease; can cause AV block, but not
dilated

cardiomyopathy with travel to Bolivia.

•

B. Echinococcus granulosus → Hydatid cysts (mainly liver/lung).

•

C. Treponema pallidum → Syphilis; can cause aortitis but not
bi-fascicular

block + DCM.

•

D. Leishmania brasiliensis → Causes mucocutaneous leishmaniasis, not
cardiac

disease.

•

E. Trypanosoma cruzi → Classic cause of Chagas disease → dilated

cardiomyopathy, conduction defects, apical aneurysm, sudden death.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Chagas disease = Latin America (Bolivia, Brazil).

•

Organism = Trypanosoma cruzi.

•

Cardiac features: dilated cardiomyopathy, conduction defects,
arrhythmias,

apical aneurysm.

•

Other features: megaesophagus, megacolon.

Infectious Causes of Cardiomyopathy & Conduction Disease

Infection / Organism Mechanism Cardiac Manifestations Buzzwords / Clues

Trypanosoma cruzi

(Chagas disease)

Protozoan parasite, destroys

myocardial cells & conduction

pathways

Dilated cardiomyopathy, apical

aneurysm, conduction blocks (bi-/

tri-fascicular), sudden death

Bolivia/Brazil, reduviid "kissing

bug", megaesophagus,

megacolon

Borrelia burgdorferi

(Lyme disease)

Spirochete, inflammation of

conduction system

AV block (fluctuating), myocarditis,

pericarditis

Tick bite, erythema migrans,

USA/Europe

Coxsackievirus B Viral myocarditis Dilated cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias

Young adult with viral

prodrome → heart failure

HIV

Direct + secondary infections

(toxoplasma, CMV)

Dilated cardiomyopathy, pericardial

effusion

Advanced immunosuppression

Diphtheria

(Corynebacterium

diphtheriae)

Toxin-mediated myocardial

necrosis

Myocarditis, AV block,

arrhythmias

Throat pseudomembranes,

neuropathy

Treponema pallidum

(Syphilis)

Endarteritis of vasa vasorum

Aortitis → Aortic regurgitation,

aneurysm

Late syphilis, "tree-bark" aorta

Toxoplasma gondii

Opportunistic myocarditis in

immunocompromised

Myocarditis, conduction defects HIV, congenital infection

Chagas vs Lyme

(contrast)

Chagas → chronic DCM +

conduction disease

Lyme → transient fluctuating AV

block

Geography is key (Latin

America vs USA/Europe)

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Latin America + DCM + conduction disease = Chagas (T. cruzi).

•

USA/Europe + AV block after tick bite = Lyme (Borrelia).

•

Viral myocarditis (Coxsackie) = young → dilated cardiomyopathy.

•

Diphtheria = myocarditis + neuropathy.

•

Syphilis = aortic regurgitation, aneurysm.

Mnemonic: "Big Crazy Love Story"

Borrelia → AV block

•

Cruzi → DCM + conduction block

•

Lyme → AV block

•

Syphilis → Aortitis

stem: Prostatitis (DRE: Tender prostate) Rx?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Ciprofloxacin

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Acute bacterial prostatitis → presents with fever, dysuria, pelvic pain,
tender

prostate on DRE.

•

Rx requires an antibiotic that penetrates the prostate well.

•

Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) and trimethoprim are the

preferred agents because of good prostatic tissue penetration.

•

Duration: typically, 4 weeks (longer than simple UTI).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Cefalexin → Poor prostatic penetration.

•

Clarithromycin → Not used; poor coverage of typical urinary pathogens
(E. coli,

Enterobacteriaceae).

•

Augmentin (amoxicillin-clavulanate) → Limited penetration, not
first-line.

•

Trimethoprim → Effective, but fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin) are often

first-line due to broader coverage and higher tissue levels.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

Acute prostatitis Rx = Ciprofloxacin (or

trimethoprim if FQ

contraindicated).

•

Always avoid prostatic massage in acute prostatitis → risk of
bacteraemia /

sepsis.

stem: A 32 yr old female with Crohn's and right hemicolectomy came with non-bloody diarrhoea. ESR, CRP and platelet were normal. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Correct Answer

A. Cholestyramine

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Crohn's disease + right hemicolectomy.

•

Now presenting with non-bloody diarrhoea.

•

ESR, CRP, platelets = normal → excludes active inflammatory flare.

•

After ileal/right colon resection → bile acid malabsorption is a common
cause

of chronic watery diarrhoea.

•

Treatment: Bile acid sequestrants (Cholestyramine).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

B. Metronidazole → Used in infective or perianal Crohn's, not here.

•

C. Mesalazine → Anti-inflammatory for active Crohn's/UC flares, but not

effective for bile acid diarrhoea.

•

D. Omeprazole → Acid suppression, no role in this case.

•

E. Prednisolone → Used for Crohn's flare, but markers are normal (no
active

inflammation).

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Post-ileal resection diarrhoea + normal inflammatory markers = bile acid

diarrhoea.

•

Treatment = bile acid sequestrants (Cholestyramine, Colesevelam).

stem: Severe pulmonary stenosis — what does the JVP waveform show?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Giant a waves

Key Points from the Scenario

Severe pulmonary stenosis → obstruction at the pulmonary valve → right

ventricular hypertrophy → impaired emptying of the right atrium into the
RV.

•

This leads to increased resistance to right atrial contraction →
produces

giant 'a' waves in the JVP.

•

Canonical waves (a.k.a. cannon waves) occur when the atria contract
against

a closed tricuspid valve, typically in complete heart block, VT, or AV

dissociation.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Giant a waves → pulmonary stenosis, pulmonary hypertension, tricuspid

stenosis.

•

Cannon waves → AV dissociation (complete heart block, VT).

🫀 JVP Wave Abnormalities

Wave Normal physiology Abnormal pattern Causes Buzzword Clue

a wave RA contraction Giant a wave

Pulmonary stenosis, Pulmonary

HTN, Tricuspid stenosis

"RA contracts against stiff

RV"

Absent a wave Atrial fibrillation "No atrial contraction"

c wave

Bulging of tricuspid into

RA during RV systole

Not usually pathologic ---

Small, not clinically

prominent

v wave

RA filling against closed

tricuspid valve

Giant v wave Tricuspid regurgitation "Systolic surge in JVP"

Cannon a

wave

RA contraction vs closed

tricuspid (AV dissociation)

Irregular giant waves

Complete heart block, VT, AV

dissociation

"Atria contract against

closed valve"

y descent RA emptying into RV Steep y descent Constrictive pericarditis
"Rapid fall, dip"

Slow y descent Tricuspid stenosis, RA myxoma "Obstructed emptying"

x descent RA relaxation Prominent x descent

Tamponade, constrictive

pericarditis

"Deep fall"

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Giant a waves → Pulmonary stenosis, Pulmonary HTN, Tricuspid stenosis.

•

Absent a wave → Atrial fibrillation.

•

Cannon waves → Complete heart block, VT, AV dissociation.

•

Giant v waves → Tricuspid regurgitation.

•

Steep y descent → Constrictive pericarditis

45 y/o woman presented with 6 month H/O pain and swelling in knees and
DIP joints

of hand.

Early morning stiffness eased at around lunch hour. ESR 40.

Dx?

Generalised nodal OA

Gout

SLE

PsA

RA

ANSWERS:

RA (?)

Correct Answer

RA (Rheumatoid Arthritis)

Key Points from the Scenario

•

45-year-old woman → common age group for RA.

•

6 months of pain + swelling in knees + hand joints.

•

Early morning stiffness lasting until around lunch (\~several hours) →

hallmark of inflammatory arthritis (esp. RA).

•

ESR 40 (elevated) → supports inflammation.

•

Distribution:

o

DIPs are less common in RA (PIPs and MCPs more classic).

o

But RA can involve multiple small and large joints symmetrically with

prolonged stiffness.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Generalised nodal OA → DIP involvement is classic, but stiffness is
brief (\<30

min), improves with activity.

•

Gout → Acute, episodic, usually 1st MTP, not chronic symmetric swelling.

•

SLE → Arthralgia common, but usually non-erosive, with systemic features
(rash,

cytopenias).

•

Psoriatic arthritis → Can involve DIPs, but usually with psoriasis, nail
pitting,

dactylitis --- not mentioned here.

•

RA → Prolonged early morning stiffness, systemic inflammation, multiple
joints

involved, elevated ESR.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Morning stiffness \<30 min → OA.

•

Morning stiffness \>1 hr → RA or other inflammatory arthritis.

•

DIP + psoriasis/nails → PsA.

•

Big toe acute attack → Gout.

stem: A 67 y/o man 4 week history of left foot drop, right hand and left foot numbness, weight loss of 10 kg, polymyalgia, polyarthralgia, temp of 38.6, Hypertensive. Diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)

Key Points from the Scenario

•

67 y/o man with systemic illness:

o

Neuropathy → left foot drop (mononeuritis multiplex) + numbness.

o

Systemic features → fever, weight loss, polyarthralgia.

o

Hypertension → common in PAN due to renal artery involvement.

•

Time course (4 weeks) and constellation of

neurological + systemic +

vascular signs strongly point to medium-vessel vasculitis (PAN).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

GCA (Giant Cell Arteritis) → Usually causes headache, jaw claudication,
visual

loss, scalp tenderness; not neuropathy or polyarthralgia in this
pattern.

•

Paraneoplastic syndrome → Could cause neuropathy and weight loss, but

would not explain fever + hypertension + polyarthralgia together.

•

SLE → Multisystem, but usually with rash, cytopenias, nephritis,
serositis; not

classically foot drop with hypertension.

•

PAN → Classic exam scenario: mononeuritis

multiplex + fever + weight loss

hypertension + arthralgia.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

PAN = Medium-vessel vasculitis → systemic illness with neuropathy,
renal

HTN, abdominal pain, arthralgia.

•

Strongly associated with Hepatitis B.

•

Buzzword: Mononeuritis multiplex + HTN + weight loss.

stem: A 19 year old male at clinic for assessment of tall stature On examination small gonads + 47 XXY Which additional feature most specific to this condition?
explanation:
Correct Answer

b\) Gynaecomastia

Key Points from the Scenario

•

19 y/o male, tall stature, small gonads, karyotype 47 XXY → Klinefelter

syndrome.

•

Features of Klinefelter's:

o

Tall stature, long limbs.

o

Small firm testes (primary hypogonadism).

o

Infertility.

o

Gynaecomastia → most specific and characteristic due to ↑

oestrogen:androgen ratio.

o

Learning difficulties may also be present.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

a\) Anosmia → Seen in Kallmann syndrome (hypogonadotropic

hypogonadism).

•

c\) Hypospadias → Congenital urogenital malformation, not linked to

Klinefelter's.

•

d\) Hypertelorism → Wide-spaced eyes, associated with genetic syndromes

(e.g., Noonan), not Klinefelter's.

•

e\) Increased muscle mass → Opposite: patients often have reduced muscle

bulk due to hypogonadism.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) = Tall male + small testes + infertility +

gynaecomastia.

•

Most specific feature = gynaecomastia (risk of breast cancer ↑).

•

Metoclopramide → acute dystonia (oculogyric crisis, torticollis,

•

Treatment = Anticholinergic (Procyclidine or Benztropine) IM/IV.

stem: A 78 y/o with iPD, dying. Rotigotine caused delusion and hallucinations for him. What will you give for worsening rigidity?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Midazolam S/C infusion

Key Points from the Scenario

•

78 y/o with idiopathic Parkinson's disease (iPD), end of life care.

•

Rotigotine (dopamine agonist) → hallucinations & delusions → stopped.

•

Patient now has worsening rigidity in the dying phase.

•

In end-of-life palliative care for Parkinson's disease:

o

Usual Parkinson's drugs (dopamine agonists, levodopa) are often

stopped due to poor tolerance, swallowing issues, or side effects

(hallucinations).

o

Symptom control becomes priority.

o

Subcutaneous Midazolam infusion is used for muscle rigidity,

restlessness, and distress.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Lorazepam tabs → Oral not appropriate in dying patient (swallowing
issues).

•

Morphine infusion → Used for pain or dyspnoea, not rigidity.

•

Oxycodone infusion → Opioid for pain, not rigidity.

•

NG for Meds → Inappropriate in the terminal phase, burdensome and not

recommended for comfort care.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

End-of-life iPD management:

o

Stop Parkinson's drugs if not tolerated.

o

Treat rigidity/distress with SC Midazolam.

o

Opioids reserved for pain/dyspnoea, not rigidity.

•

Midazolam SC = rigidity + agitation in dying PD patients.

A 78 y/o presents with 3 days of fever, malaise, SOB, cough. CXR showed
RLL

Consolidation.

Hb 11.2, TW 29.4, Lymphocyte 18.4. Neutrophil 9.5, Eos 0.4, Basophil
0.1.

What investigations to do next?

Immunophenotyping of WBC

Bone marrow aspirate

CT abdominal

Mantoux

Bone marrow cytogenetics

ANSWERS:

Immunophenotyping of WBC

Correct Answer

Immunophenotyping of WBC

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Elderly patient (78 y/o) with fever, pneumonia (RLL consolidation).

•

Bloods:

o

Hb: 11.2 (mild anaemia).

o

WCC: 29.4 (marked leukocytosis).

o

Lymphocytes: 18.4 (absolute lymphocytosis).

o

Neutrophils: 9.5 (slightly raised).

•

Marked lymphocytosis in an elderly patient → suspicious for chronic

lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL).

•

Next step: Peripheral blood immunophenotyping (flow cytometry) →

confirms clonality of B-lymphocytes (CD5+,

CD19+, CD23+ → diagnostic for

CLL).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Bone marrow aspirate → Not first-line; immunophenotyping from peripheral

blood is diagnostic.

•

CT abdomen → Useful later to assess lymphadenopathy, organomegaly,

staging --- not initial.

•

Mantoux → Tuberculosis test, irrelevant here.

•

Bone marrow cytogenetics → Done for prognosis (e.g., 17p deletion), but
after

diagnosis is confirmed.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Elderly + lymphocytosis = suspect CLL.

•

First diagnostic step = immunophenotyping of peripheral blood.

•

Bone marrow biopsy not needed for diagnosis, only for staging/prognosis.

stem: 20 y/o IVDU, presents with 2wks of Fever, loss of weight, pleuritic Chest Pain and SOB. CXR showed right pleural effusion. What would be the next investigations?
explanation:
Correct Answer

US Chest

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Young IVDU (IV drug user) → high risk of infective endocarditis → septic

emboli → pleural effusion / empyema.

•

CXR shows right pleural effusion → the immediate next step is to

characterize and sample the effusion.

•

Ultrasound chest is the safest and best next investigation:

o

Confirms presence of pleural fluid.

o

Guides diagnostic aspiration (thoracocentesis).

o

Differentiates free vs loculated fluid.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Bronchoscopy → not indicated initially; used for airway obstruction,

haemoptysis, or endobronchial pathology.

•

Lateral CXR → may confirm effusion, but less useful than ultrasound
(obsolete

compared to modern imaging).

•

Thoracoscopy → invasive; reserved for undiagnosed exudates or suspected

malignancy after aspiration.

•

CT Chest → useful for parenchymal/mediastinal disease, but effusion must
be

tapped first for diagnosis.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Pleural effusion on CXR → Ultrasound-guided diagnostic aspiration = next

step.

•

Always determine if transudate vs exudate (Light's criteria) to guide

68 y/o with 1 Day History of headache, Blurring

of vision. On Examination, Right eye is

injected, hazy cornea, irregular pupil.

What is the most appropriate next step?

⁃ ESR

⁃ IO Pressure measurement

⁃ MRI B

⁃ US Eye

⁃ Visual Evoked Potential

ANSWERS:

IO Pressure measurement

Correct Answer

IO Pressure measurement

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Acute presentation: sudden headache + blurred vision.

•

Eye findings: injected conjunctiva, hazy cornea, irregular pupil →
classic for

acute angle-closure glaucoma.

•

In this condition:

o

Intraocular pressure (IOP) rises sharply.

o

Leads to corneal oedema (hazy cornea), mid-dilated irregular pupil,

severe pain, nausea/vomiting.

•

Next step: confirm diagnosis with intraocular pressure measurement →

urgent ophthalmology referral.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

ESR → used to assess temporal arteritis, but the eye signs here (hazy
cornea +

irregular pupil) are not typical.

•

MRI Brain → not indicated in an acute red eye scenario.

US Eye → may be used in retinal/vitreous pathology, not in suspected
acute

glaucoma.

•

Visual Evoked Potential → used in optic nerve disorders (e.g., MS), not
acute

glaucoma.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Acute angle-closure glaucoma = ophthalmic emergency.

•

IOP measurement is diagnostic → treatment involves acetazolamide,
topical

beta-blocker, pilocarpine, and urgent ophthalmology intervention (laser

iridotomy).

stem: 45 year old IVDU with fever, back pain, L5 tenderness. Weakness of ankle dorsiflexion. Reduced pinprick over medial aspect of leg. Which nerve root?
explanation:
Correct Answer

L4

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Weakness of ankle dorsiflexion → classically L4 or L5 root.

•

Sensory loss: medial leg → L4 dermatome (L5 is dorsum of foot + first
web

space).

•

Reflexes: knee jerk = L4 root, here only elicited with reinforcement
(weak/↓).

So, the combined pattern = L4 radiculopathy

Why Not L5?

•

L5 root → weakness of dorsiflexion too, but sensory loss is on dorsum of
foot

and big toe web space, not medial leg.

•

Reflex involvement: L5 has no direct reflex, unlike L4 (knee jerk).

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

L4 root → knee jerk, medial leg sensory, dorsiflexion.

•

L5 root → dorsiflexion + big toe extension, dorsum foot sensory, no
reflex.

•

S1 root → ankle jerk, lateral foot sensory, plantarflexion.

stem: An 80 y/o with 6 months of central blurring of vision, smoking with no improvement on pinhole. VA = 6/18 Dx?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Macular degeneration

Key Points from the Scenario

•

80-year-old smoker → strongest risk factor for age-related macular

degeneration (AMD).

•

Gradual, central blurring of vision → hallmark of macular pathology.

•

No improvement with pinhole → suggests retinal pathology, not refractive

error.

•

Visual acuity 6/18 → moderate visual impairment, typical of AMD
progression.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Glaucoma → Causes peripheral field loss first, central vision affected
late.

•

Charles Bonnet syndrome → Visual hallucinations in people with poor
vision,

not a cause of blurring itself.

•

Cataract → Causes generalised blurring and glare, often improves with

pinhole, not central vision loss alone.

•

Post-cortical atrophy → Neurological/Alzheimer's variant, causes
higher-order

visual dysfunction, not isolated central blur.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Central vision loss + smoker + elderly → Age-related Macular

Degeneration (AMD).

•

Glaucoma = peripheral loss first.

•

Cataract = global blur, glare, improves with pinhole.

stem: A 60 year hypertensive pt was on amlodipine but developed ankle oedema. Changed to Chlorthalidone. Mechanism of action of Chlorthalidone?
explanation:
Correct Answer

C\) Na-Cl co-transporter inhibition

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Chlorthalidone = thiazide-like diuretic.

•

Used for hypertension, mild heart failure, oedema.

•

Mechanism:

o

Acts on the distal convoluted tubule.

o

Inhibits the Na⁺-Cl⁻ co-transporter → ↑ Na⁺ and water excretion.

o

Also causes ↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption → useful in calcium stones,

osteoporosis

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

A\) ENaC channel activation → Wrong direction; amiloride/triamterene act
by

ENaC inhibition in collecting duct.

•

B\) Renin inhibition → Aliskiren is the renin inhibitor.

•

D\) Na-K-2Cl cotransporter inhibition → Loop diuretics (furosemide,

bumetanide) in thick ascending limb.

•

E\) Stimulation of ANP → Not the mechanism of any standard

antihypertensive/diuretic.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Chlorthalidone/Thiazides → inhibit Na-Cl cotransporter in DCT.

•

Side effects: Hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia,

hypercalcaemia,

hyperuricaemia, hyperglycaemia, dyslipidaemia.

stem: A 24 y/o present with abdominal pain, nausea & vomiting. No Bowel Output. Which drug is the culprit?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Lithium

Key Points from the Scenario

•

24-year-old with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, no bowel output →

classic for intestinal obstruction-like picture due to lithium-induced

paralytic ileus.

•

Lithium toxicity/adverse effects include:

o

GI: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea/constipation, ileus.

o

Neuro: tremor, confusion, ataxia, seizures.

o

Renal: nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, CKD.

o

Endocrine: hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Amisulpride → Antipsychotic; causes hyperprolactinaemia, QT
prolongation,

EPS.

•

Clobazam → Benzodiazepine; causes sedation, tolerance, dependence.

•

Valproate → Hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, weight gain, teratogenicity;
not ileus.

•

Clonazepam → Benzodiazepine; sedation, ataxia, but no bowel obstruction.

High-Yield Key Concepts:

•

Lithium → paralytic ileus + hypothyroidism + nephrogenic DI + tremor.

•

Always check serum lithium levels in such presentations.

Lithium: Adverse Effects

System Adverse Effect Exam Buzzword

GI Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, paralytic ileus

"Abdominal pain, no bowel

output → lithium"

Renal

Polyuria, polydipsia, nephrogenic diabetes

insipidus, chronic

tubulointerstitial nephritis

"CKD in long-term lithium use"

"Tremor that worsens with

toxicity"

Endocrine

hypercalcaemia

"Goitre on lithium"

Pregnancy

"Lithium in 1st trimester"

High-Yield Exam Pearls

•

Therapeutic range: 0.6--1.2 mmol/L (toxicity \>1.5 mmol/L).

•

Monitor: U&E, TFT, calcium, lithium levels every 3 months.

•

Drug interactions ↑ lithium: Thiazides, ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs.

•

Acute toxicity signs: GI upset + tremor + confusion.

Mnemonic: "LiTHIUM"

•

L → Lethargy (neuro)

•

i → Increased TSH (hypothyroidism)

•

T → Tremor / Teratogen (Ebstein anomaly)

•

H → Hypercalcaemia (↑ PTH)

•

I → Ileus (paralytic)

•

U → Urinary problems (nephrogenic DI)

•

M → Mind (neurotoxicity, seizures)

stem: Specificity definition — best statement?
options: Proportion of people without disease who test negative (True negative rate)
Proportion of tested negatives who truly don't have disease (NPV)
Proportion of people with disease who test positive
Probability that a positive test is a true positive
Proportion of true positives among all positives
explanation:
Definition of Specificity

Specificity = ability of a test to correctly identify those without
the disease (true

negatives).

So, if a test has 98% specificity, it means:

98% of patients without coeliac disease will have a negative test.

Why the Other Option is Wrong

•

"98% of the tested negative don't have the disease"

o

That describes the Negative Predictive Value (NPV), not specificity.

o

NPV depends on prevalence of the disease in the population.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Specificity → True negative rate = proportion of healthy people
correctly

identified as disease-free.

•

Sensitivity → True positive rate = proportion of

diseased people correctly

identified.

•

Predictive values (PPV, NPV) depend on prevalence, while

sensitivity/specificity do not.

Mnemonic:

•

"SPIN" = SPecific test when Positive rules IN disease.

•

"SNOUT" = SeNsitive test when Negative rules OUT disease.

Test Characteristics

Concept Definition Formula Exam Clue / Example

Sensitivity

Probability that a test correctly

identifies patients with the disease

TP / (TP +

FN)

"Highly sensitive test → few false negatives

→ rules OUT (SNOUT)." e.g. D-dimer for PE.

Specificity

Probability that a test correctly

identifies patients without the

disease

TN / (TN +

FP)

"Highly specific test → few false positives →

rules IN (SPIN)." e.g. Anti-endomysial Ab

for coeliac.

Positive Predictive

Value (PPV)

Probability that a patient who tests

positive actually has the disease

TP / (TP +

FP)

"Out of all positive results, how many are

true?" Depends on prevalence.

Negative

Predictive Value

(NPV)

Probability that a patient who tests

negative truly does not have the

disease

TN / (TN +

FN)

"Out of all negative results, how many are

true?" Also, prevalence-dependent.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Sensitivity & Specificity → intrinsic properties of the test (don't
change with

PPV & NPV → depend on prevalence (↑ prevalence = ↑ PPV, ↓ NPV).

•

Gold standard tests are usually high specificity, while screening tests
are

usually high sensitivity.

Mnemonic:

•

SNOUT = SeNsitive test, Negative → rules OUT.

•

SPIN = SPecific test, Positive → rules IN.

Correct Answer

DC Cardioversion

Key Points from the Scenario

Young man with palpitations & sweating → Symptomatic arrhythmia.

extreme, but significant.

ECG: Broad QRS Complex Tachycardia (QRS = 150 ms) → Suggests

ventricular tachycardia (VT) until proven otherwise.

MRCP Syndrome Key Points: Any broad complex tachycardia with
hemodynamic

instability = immediate DC cardioversion.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer

In the ACLS/ALS and MRCP exam context, broad complex tachycardia is
presumed

to be ventricular tachycardia (VT) unless clearly proven otherwise.

•

The presence of hypotension (90/60) indicates hemodynamic instability.

•

In such cases, drugs like amiodarone or flecainide are not first-line.
They

may be considered only in stable VT.

•

DC cardioversion (synchronized electrical cardioversion) is the safest,
most

effective, and exam-preferred management for unstable VT.

•

This is a high-yield concept: "Unstable tachyarrhythmia → Shock first."

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Amiodarone

▪ Used in stable broad complex tachycardia (VT).

▪ In this patient, instability (low BP + symptoms) makes electrical
therapy

mandatory.

▪ Giving amiodarone wastes time and risks cardiac arrest.

Flecainide

▪ A Class IC antiarrhythmic, used in supraventricular arrhythmias
(like

atrial fibrillation in structurally normal hearts).

▪ Contraindicated in structural heart disease, ischemia, or VT.

▪ Not used in broad complex tachycardia (especially when unstable).

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Unstable tachycardia (hypotension, chest pain, heart failure, syncope)
→

DC cardioversion

•

Stable broad complex tachycardia → Amiodarone (IV infusion)

•

Flecainide is for SVTs, not VT

stem: A 50-year-old Somalian man presented with weight loss for 4 weeks. Unilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with Rt sided consolidation. Peritoneal thickening, right sided pleural effusion. CT: Peritoneal nodes Dx?
explanation:
Correct Answer

A\) Tuberculosis (TB)

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Somalian man → High-risk background for tuberculosis (TB prevalence
higher

in African/immigrant populations).

•

Weight loss for 4 weeks → Constitutional/B symptoms → common

in TB and malignancy, less so in sarcoidosis.

•

Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy → Can be seen in sarcoidosis (classic),
TB,

and lymphoma/malignancy.

•

Right-sided consolidation + pleural effusion → Strongly

suggest infective/inflammatory pathology such as TB, less likely
sarcoid.

•

Peritoneal thickening + peritoneal nodes → Abdominal TB (peritoneal

involvement is very typical), rare in sarcoid, unusual for carcinoma.

•

Combination of chest + abdominal findings →

Classic for disseminated TB.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (TB)

The clinical picture is disseminated tuberculosis, involving:

•

Chest: hilar lymphadenopathy, lung consolidation, pleural effusion.

•

Abdomen: peritoneal thickening and lymph nodes.

•

Systemic features: weight loss, subacute onset.

This multi-system involvement across chest and abdomen is highly
characteristic of

TB, especially in someone from Somalia (high prevalence).

Sarcoidosis usually gives non-caseating granulomas, commonly hilar

lymphadenopathy and lung infiltrates, but pleural effusion and
peritoneal

thickening are rare.

Bronchial carcinoma may cause weight loss + lung mass + nodes, but
peritoneal

disease + effusion in this distribution is atypical, especially without
a dominant lung

mass.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Sarcoidosis

o

Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is classic.

o

But pleural effusion and peritoneal thickening/nodes are very unusual

in sarcoidosis.

o

Sarcoid tends to cause pulmonary fibrosis, hypercalcemia, uveitis,

erythema nodosum, not peritoneal disease.

Bronchial carcinoma

o

Could cause weight loss, hilar nodes, and lung consolidation.

o

But widespread peritoneal thickening and peritoneal lymphadenopathy

is not typical of lung carcinoma (unless advanced metastasis, but then

you'd expect a clear dominant lung lesion or liver mets first).

o

Also, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy without a clear primary mass is

less in keeping with carcinoma.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy differential: TB, sarcoidosis,
lymphoma.

•

TB clues: immigrant from high-prevalence

area, weight loss, consolidation,

pleural effusion, peritoneal involvement.

•

Sarcoid clues: young adult, African/Caribbean, dry cough, erythema
nodosum,

hypercalcemia, no effusion.

•

Bronchial carcinoma clues: smoker, dominant lung mass, hemoptysis,

metastases (liver, bone, brain).

A 65-year-old patient on long term peritoneal dialysis admitted with
fever, tachycardia

and hypotension.

Presents with abdominal pain, cloudy PD effluent

Temp 38.5

WCC: 14.5

CRP 95

What\'s the most likely organism?

E. faecalis

E. coli

Staph epidermidis

MRSA

E. Histolytica

ANSWERS:

Staph epidermidis

Correct Answer

Staphylococcus epidermidis

Key Points from the Scenario

•

65-year-old on long-term peritoneal dialysis → immediately raises
suspicion

for peritoneal dialysis--associated peritonitis

•

Fever, tachycardia, hypotension → systemic sepsis

•

Raised inflammatory markers (WCC 14.5, CRP 95) → confirms infection

•

Most likely pathogen in PD peritonitis: skin flora introduced via the

catheter

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Staphylococcus
epidermidis)

In patients on chronic peritoneal dialysis, peritonitis is a
well-recognised

complication

Most common organisms:

o

Coagulase-negative staphylococci (esp. Staph epidermidis) → from

skin contamination at catheter site.

o

Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) → also possible but less

common than Staph epidermidis.

o

Gram-negative bacilli (E. coli, Klebsiella,

Pseudomonas) → less

common, though seen in severe abdominal contamination.

•

Staph epidermidis is the single most frequent cause due to its biofilm-

forming ability on indwelling catheters.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

E. faecalis

o

Enterococcus can cause intra-abdominal infections, but not the leading

cause of PD peritonitis.

o

Usually associated with prior abdominal surgery or complicated intra-

abdominal sepsis.

E. coli

o

Common in secondary peritonitis (e.g., bowel perforation, peritoneal

contamination).

o

But in PD-associated peritonitis, Gram-positive skin organisms

predominate, not enteric Gram-negatives.

Staphylococcus epidermidis

o

Correct answer → most common cause of PD-related peritonitis due to

skin entry along catheter tract.

MRSA

o

Possible, especially in recurrent infections or known MRSA carriers.

o

But less common than coagulase-negative staph in PD peritonitis.

Entamoeba histolytica

o

Causes amoebic liver abscess and sometimes secondary peritonitis after

abscess rupture.

o

Not a cause of PD-related peritonitis.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Most common cause of peritonitis in long-term PD → Staph epidermidis

If the question mentions bowel perforation or intra-abdominal source →

think Gram-negatives like E. coli

•

If the patient is a known MRSA carrier or recurrent infections →
consider

MRSA

stem: A 35-year-old woman came with tiredness and lethargy for infertility workup. Her observations and her periods are normal. Hb 66 MCV 67 Dx?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Iron deficiency

Key Points from the Scenario

•

35-year-old woman, infertility workup → reproductive age, menstrual
loss is

a common cause of anaemia.

•

Symptoms: tiredness, lethargy → nonspecific, but consistent with
anaemia.

•

Hb 66 g/L (severe anaemia) → significant pathology.

•

MCV 67 fL (microcytic) → microcytic anaemia.

•

Differential of microcytic anaemia (low MCV):

o

Iron deficiency (most common).

o

Thalassemia trait (but usually mild anaemia, family/ethnic history).

o

Anaemia of chronic disease (usually normocytic, sometimes microcytic).

o

Sideroblastic anaemia (rare).

Normal periods and no overt bleeding are mentioned, but in exam
settings, the

default assumption in a reproductive-age woman with microcytic severe

anaemia = iron deficiency anaemia

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Iron Deficiency Anaemia)

Iron deficiency is the most common cause of microcytic anaemia
worldwide.

•

In women of childbearing age, menstrual losses or poor iron intake are
the

leading causes.

•

Severe anaemia (Hb 66) with microcytosis (MCV 67) = textbook
presentation.

•

Iron deficiency → reduced Hb synthesis → smaller red cells
(microcytosis).

•

Symptoms = fatigue, lethargy, possible infertility (iron deficiency can
impair

ovulation and implantation).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Hypothyroidism

o

Can cause anaemia (usually normocytic or macrocytic due to reduced

erythropoiesis or B12 deficiency from autoimmune gastritis).

o

Not typically microcytic.

Vitamin B12 deficiency

o

Causes macrocytic anaemia (MCV \> 100), neurological signs, glossitis.

o

Not consistent with MCV 67.

Myeloproliferative disorder

o

Usually causes normocytic or macrocytic anaemia, often associated

with leukocytosis/thrombocytosis.

o

Not a cause of isolated microcytic anaemia.

Iron deficiency

o

Fits perfectly: young woman, microcytic, severe anaemia.

Sickle cell anaemia

o

Causes normocytic or slightly microcytic anaemia, but chronic

hemolytic features (jaundice, crises, family history, ethnicity).

o

Severe isolated microcytosis without haemolysis = not sickle.

Thalassemia

o

Causes microcytic anaemia, but usually with normal or mildly reduced

Hb, and often discovered earlier in life.

o

Hb of 66 is too low for thalassemia trait (unless thalassemia major,

which presents in childhood).

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Microcytic anaemia = Iron deficiency, Thalassemia, Sideroblastic,
Chronic

disease (rarely).

Iron deficiency → reproductive-age women, low Hb, microcytosis, most

common worldwide.

•

Thalassemia trait → microcytosis but with normal or near-normal Hb.

•

B12 deficiency & Hypothyroidism → macrocytic.

•

Sickle cell → hemolytic features, not pure microcytosis.

ALTERNATIVE SCENARIO

A 35-year-old woman came with tiredness and lethargy for infertility
workup.

Her observations and her periods are normal.

Mild anaemia

Disproportionate MCV

S. Ferritin = normal

Dx?

Hypothyroidism

B12 Deficiency

Myeloproliferative disorder

Sickle cell anaemia

Thalassemia

ANSWERS:

Thalassemia

Correct Answer

Thalassemia

Key Points from the Scenario

•

35-year-old woman → reproductive age, presenting for infertility workup

(anaemia discovered incidentally).

•

Symptoms: tiredness and lethargy → nonspecific,

common with anaemia.

•

Mild anaemia → Hb not very low (contrast to severe IDA).

•

Disproportionate MCV (markedly low relative to Hb level) → classic clue

for thalassemia trait.

•

Serum ferritin normal → rules out iron deficiency.

MRCP Syndrome Pearl: Microcytosis out of proportion to the degree of
anaemia +

normal ferritin = Thalassemia trait.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Thalassemia)

•

Thalassemia trait (alpha or beta) is characterised by:

o

Mild anaemia (Hb often \>9--10 g/dL).

o

Very low MCV (often \<70 fL).

o

Normal iron stores (ferritin normal).

•

Patients are often asymptomatic, discovered during screening
(infertility

workup, antenatal screening).

•

Important for genetic counselling: if both partners are carriers, there
is a risk

of thalassemia major in offspring.

Thus, the combination of mild anaemia + low MCV disproportionate to Hb +

normal ferritin makes thalassemia the best answer.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Hypothyroidism

o

Causes normocytic or macrocytic anaemia, not microcytic.

o

No features of hypothyroidism described.

B12 deficiency

o

Causes macrocytic anaemia (MCV \>100 fL), with neurological features

and glossitis.

o

Doesn't fit here.

Myeloproliferative disorder

o

Anaemia is not usually the main presenting feature.

o

Associated with leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, splenomegaly.

o

Not suggested here.

Sickle cell anaemia

o

Normocytic or slightly microcytic haemolytic anaemia.

o

Features: jaundice, crises, family history.

o

Not consistent with this asymptomatic case.

5\. Thalassemia

o

Perfect match: mild anaemia + disproportionate microcytosis +

normal ferritin.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Microcytosis + normal ferritin = Thalassemia trait (until proven

otherwise).

•

Iron deficiency = microcytic, but with low ferritin.

•

Macrocytosis → think B12/folate deficiency, hypothyroidism, liver
disease,

alcohol, marrow disorders.

stem: Young female patient presenting with multiple episodic attacks of Vertigo, Diplopia and Tinnitus, episode lasting for about 4 hours. On examination during attack, she was found to have Right Horizontal Beating Nystagmus, Vertigo, Right ear pain and mild Right Sensorineural Hearing Loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer

4\. Ménière's Disease

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Young female → common demographic for Ménière's.

•

Multiple episodic attacks of:

o

Vertigo (lasting hours, not seconds/minutes)

o

Diplopia, tinnitus, ear pain, sensorineural hearing loss

•

Episode duration: \~4 hours → very typical of Ménière's (20 minutes --
12

hours).

•

Examination during attack: right horizontal

beating nystagmus, vertigo, right

ear pain, mild right-sided SNHL.

•

Combination of episodic vertigo + tinnitus + fluctuating SNHL =
Ménière's

triad.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Ménière's Disease)

Ménière's disease is an idiopathic inner ear disorder due to
endolymphatic

hydrops (excess endolymph fluid).

•

Classic triad:

Episodic vertigo (lasting 20 min -- 12 hours).

Sensorineural hearing loss (fluctuating, often unilateral early on).

Tinnitus ± ear fullness/aural pressure.

•

Attacks can also cause nystagmus and balance

disturbance.

•

This case fits perfectly: 4-hour vertigo episodes + tinnitus +
unilateral SNHL

nystagmus.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma)

o

Causes progressive, persistent unilateral hearing loss and imbalance,

not episodic attacks.

o

Symptoms are slowly progressive, not paroxysmal.

Labyrinthitis

o

Follows a viral/bacterial infection.

o

Causes sudden onset, prolonged vertigo (days--weeks) with hearing

loss.

Not episodic and recurrent.

3\. Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)

o

Triggered by head position changes.

o

Attacks last seconds to minutes, not hours.

o

No hearing loss or tinnitus.

4\. Ménière's Disease

o

Fits perfectly: episodic vertigo (hours), tinnitus, hearing loss,
nystagmus.

5\. Vestibular schwannoma (same as acoustic neuroma)

o

See point 1 above: progressive, not episodic.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

BPPV → seconds--minutes, positional, no hearing loss.

•

Labyrinthitis → single prolonged attack (days--weeks), post-infectious,
with

hearing loss.

•

Ménière's → recurrent attacks lasting hours, with hearing loss +
tinnitus.

•

Vestibular schwannoma → progressive, persistent unilateral SNHL ±

imbalance.

stem: A young woman with history sudden unexplained blackouts, similar history one month back. O/E: ECG = normal 24 hr ambulatory ECG = No arrythmia What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
Correct Answer

2\. Internal loop recorder

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Young woman with recurrent sudden unexplained blackouts → concerning

for cardiac syncope.

•

Baseline ECG normal → no resting conduction abnormalities.

•

24-hour ambulatory ECG showed no arrhythmia → so episodes are too

infrequent to be captured by short-term Holter monitoring.

•

Need a test that can correlate symptoms with rhythm over a longer
period.

•

Internal loop recorder provides long-term monitoring (months to

years) and is indicated when blackouts are recurrent but infrequent.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Internal Loop Recorder)

•

In patients with unexplained syncope, arrhythmia is often suspected, but
if

events are rare (not daily), standard 24--72 hr Holter or event monitors
may miss

them.

•

An implantable/internal loop recorder sits subcutaneously and can record

ECG for up to 2--3 years.

•

It auto-activates with abnormal rhythms or can be patient-triggered
during

symptoms.

•

NICE and ESC guidelines recommend it for

recurrent unexplained syncope

where arrhythmia is suspected and non-invasive tests are unrevealing.

•

In this case → perfect choice because events are infrequent (one
blackout a

month).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

One-week recorder

o

Provides only a short window of monitoring.

o

May still miss arrhythmia if blackouts are infrequent (as in this
case).

Internal loop recorder

o

Correct: best for rare, unexplained syncope with normal ECG and

negative Holter.

72-hour ambulatory ECG

o

Same limitation as above → still too short, likely to miss the event.

48-hour ambulatory ECG

Also too short, only useful if symptoms occur daily or every 2--3 days.

5\. Electrophysiology study (EPS)

o

Invasive test used if structural heart disease or strong suspicion of

arrhythmogenic syncope.

o

With a normal ECG and no arrhythmia on monitoring, this is premature.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Frequent symptoms (daily/weekly) → Holter /

event monitor

•

Infrequent, unexplained syncope → Internal loop recorder

•

Known structural heart disease + abnormal ECG → Consider EPS

Syncope: Choosing the Right ECG Monitoring Test

Step 1. Baseline assessment

•

ECG, echocardiogram, blood tests

•

Rule out structural / obvious cardiac cause

Step 2. Event Frequency

👉 Symptoms daily / every 2--3 days

➡ 24--48 hr Holter monitor

👉 Symptoms weekly

➡ 72 hr Holter OR 7-day external event recorder

👉 Symptoms monthly or less frequent

➡ Implantable/Internal loop recorder (ILR)

Step 3. Special Situations

•

Structural heart disease / abnormal baseline ECG + strong suspicion of

arrhythmia

➡ Consider Electrophysiology Study (EPS)

•

High-risk features (syncope during exertion, family history of sudden

death, sustained VT on monitoring)

➡ Urgent admission + cardiology input

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Normal ECG + recurrent but rare blackouts → ILR is best.

•

Holter useful only when symptoms are frequent.

•

EPS is not a screening tool; it's used when there's a strong suspicion
of

arrhythmia after initial workup.

Mnemonic for recall: "FREQ → TEST"

•

Frequent (daily) → Forty-eight hr Holter

•

Regular (weekly) → Recorder (7-day)

•

Episodic (monthly) → Embedded Loop Recorder

•

Question of structural heart disease → Quick EPS

stem: A 56-year-old man presented with periumbilical abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea H/O MI, COPD, T2DM. Had admission 6 weeks ago and was treated for chest infection O/E: tender abdomen all over but no peritonitis, BP 104/77 mmHg, HR 82 bpm, T 37.2 Dx?
explanation:
Correct Answer

3\. Ischaemic colitis

Key Points from the Scenario

•

56-year-old man → middle-aged, vascular risk factors relevant.

•

Symptoms: periumbilical abdominal pain + diarrhoea → suggests colonic

pathology.

•

Past medical history:

o

MI (coronary artery disease) → atherosclerosis, vascular compromise.

o

COPD & chest infection 2 months back → recent illness, possible

hypotension/sepsis episodes.

•

Examination: abdominal tenderness but vitals stable → localized colonic

ischaemia without shock.

•

The presence of vascular risk + abdominal pain + diarrhoea strongly

suggests ischaemic colitis.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Ischaemic Colitis)

•

Ischaemic colitis is the most common form of

intestinal ischaemia.

•

Typically occurs in older patients with vascular disease (CAD, PAD,
smoking,

diabetes, COPD).

•

Pathophysiology: hypoperfusion of "watershed areas" of colon (splenic
flexure,

rectosigmoid).

•

Symptoms:

o

Sudden crampy abdominal pain (often left-sided, but may be

periumbilical).

o

Diarrhoea (sometimes bloody).

o

Abdominal tenderness.

•

Vitals may be normal or only mildly affected if segmental ischaemia.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Crohn's disease

o

Chronic relapsing illness, often younger patients.

o

Associated with weight loss, perianal disease, strictures, not acute

vascular history.

o

No mention of chronicity or extraintestinal features.

Ulcerative colitis

Younger onset, chronic course.

o

Causes bloody diarrhoea, urgency, tenesmus.

o

Not an acute isolated abdominal pain in an older man with vascular risk.

3\. Ischaemic colitis

o

Fits best: age, vascular history, acute onset abdominal pain +
diarrhoea.

4\. Diverticulitis

o

Presents with left iliac fossa pain, fever, raised WCC.

o

Diarrhoea less common, usually constipation or localized peritonism.

o

No mention of LIF pain or sepsis.

5\. Pseudomembranous colitis (C. difficile)

o

Recent antibiotic use is key.

o

Causes profuse watery diarrhoea, systemic toxicity.

o

Not suggested here (recent infection 2 months ago but no antibiotic link

provided).

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Ischaemic colitis → older patient, vascular risk factors, sudden
abdominal pain

diarrhoea (± bloody).

•

Diverticulitis → LIF pain, fever, constipation, elderly.

•

Pseudomembranous colitis → recent antibiotics, watery diarrhoea,
fever,

leukocytosis.

•

IBD (Crohn's/UC) → chronic relapsing illness in young adults.

stem: A 35-years-old presents with 2wks diarrhoea abdominal pain, Lost5kg. No Blood in stool. Had abdominal operation 6 months ago due to ruptured appendix & abscess collection. H/O GERD & was taking Omeprazole Hb 10.5, CRP 40. Faecal calprotectin 300. Anti TTGH 10 Dx?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Crohn's disease

Key Points from the Scenario

•

35-year-old with 2 weeks of diarrhoea + abdominal pain + 5 kg weight

loss → suggests an organic pathology, not IBS.

•

No blood in stool → IBD still possible (Crohn's may cause non-bloody

diarrhoea).

•

Past surgical history: ruptured appendix & abscess → Crohn's can mimic

appendicitis and cause post-op complications.

•

Medication: Omeprazole (PPI) → associated with microscopic colitis,
but less

likely given systemic features and weight loss.

•

Investigations:

o

Hb 10.5 (anaemia) → chronic inflammatory disease.

o

CRP 40 (raised) → inflammation, rules out IBS.

o

Faecal calprotectin 300 (elevated) → indicates intestinal inflammation

(IBD).

o

Anti-TTG 10 (normal, not elevated) → excludes coeliac disease.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Crohn's disease)

•

Crohn's disease often presents with:

o

Diarrhoea (may be bloody or non-bloody).

o

Abdominal pain.

o

Weight loss, anaemia, raised CRP.

o

History of "appendicitis" surgery is a classic exam clue → many
Crohn's

cases initially misdiagnosed as appendicitis due to ileocaecal

inflammation.

•

The combination of weight loss + raised CRP + high faecal calprotectin
+

past appendicitis surgery makes Crohn's the best fit.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Crohn's disease

o

Fits perfectly: systemic features, inflammation, previous
appendicitis-type

surgery, raised calprotectin.

Bile acid malabsorption

Can occur post-ileal resection or cholecystectomy.

o

Causes chronic watery diarrhoea but does not cause raised CRP or

elevated calprotectin.

o

stem: A 72 years-old fair skinned female on shin, erythematous, hyperkeratotic plaque, 2cm in diameter, lesion with scaling having scalloped edge Dx?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma in situ (Bowen's disease)
explanation:
Correct Answer

Squamous cell carcinoma in situ (Bowen's disease)

72-year-old fair-skinned female → elderly, sun-damaged skin → high risk
for

actinic/precancerous lesions.

•

Site: shin → sun-exposed area.

•

Erythematous, hyperkeratotic plaque with scaling, scalloped edge, 2 cm →

classic description of Bowen's disease (SCC in situ).

•

Lesion is plaque-like, scaly, red, keratotic rather

than a nodule or pigmented

lesion.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (SCC in situ / Bowen's
disease)

•

Squamous cell carcinoma in situ (Bowen's disease) is an intraepidermal

SCC that has not invaded the dermis.

•

Appears as:

o

Well-demarcated erythematous plaque.

o

Hyperkeratotic/scaly surface.

o

May have scalloped or irregular edges.

•

Risk factors: chronic sun exposure, fair skin, older age,
immunosuppression,

HPV.

•

Differentiates from invasive SCC by being confined to epidermis.

This lesion description is classic for SCC in situ rather than melanoma
or BCC.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Malignant melanoma

o

Usually pigmented, irregular borders, colour variation, rapid change

(ABCDE rule).

o

Not described here (no pigmentation, scaling instead).

Seborrheic keratosis

o

Waxy, "stuck-on" appearance, brown/black, benign.

o

Not erythematous or scaly with scalloped edges.

SCC in situ (Bowen's disease)

o

Fits perfectly: scaly erythematous plaque, elderly fair-skinned, sun-

exposed site.

Basal cell carcinoma (BCC)

o

Pearly nodule, rolled edges, telangiectasia, may ulcerate ("rodent
ulcer").

o

Not a flat, scaly erythematous plaque.

Bowen's disease (SCC in situ) → red, scaly, hyperkeratotic plaque on
sun-

exposed skin.

•

BCC → pearly nodule with rolled edge +

telangiectasia.

•

Melanoma → pigmented, ABCDE features.

•

Seborrheic keratosis → waxy, stuck-on, benign.

stem: A Patient with paranoid psychosis taking risperidone H/O Raynaud's with dry mouth, dysphagia Anti Smith positive Anti Ro positive Decreased C4 Dx?
explanation:
Correct Answer

SLE (Systemic Lupus Erythematosus)

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Psychosis on risperidone → could be neuropsychiatric lupus (psychosis,

seizures, depression).

Raynaud's phenomenon → can be seen in SLE, systemic sclerosis,
Sjögren's,

MCTD.

•

Dry mouth, dysphagia → sicca features (Sjögren's overlap possible).

•

Antibodies:

o

Anti-Smith positive → highly specific for SLE.

o

Anti-Ro positive → seen in both Sjögren's and SLE.

•

Complement low (↓C4) → hypocomplementemia is a strong marker of

active SLE, not systemic sclerosis or primary Sjögren's.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (SLE)

•

SLE diagnosis hinges on specific autoantibodies:

o

Anti-Smith → virtually diagnostic of SLE (though sensitivity is low).

o

Anti-Ro can be present in overlap or subacute cutaneous lupus.

•

Low complement (C3/C4) → hallmark of active immune complex--mediated

SLE (renal, neuro, systemic disease).

•

Neuropsychiatric lupus explains her paranoid psychosis.

•

Raynaud's + sicca symptoms are seen in overlap syndromes, but the
antibody

complement profile strongly point to SLE.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Systemic sclerosis

o

Would cause Raynaud's + dysphagia.

o

But would expect anti-Scl-70 or anticentromere antibodies, not anti-

Smith.

o

Low C4 is not typical.

SLE

o

Fits perfectly: psychosis, Raynaud's, anti-Smith, anti-Ro, ↓C4.

Sjögren syndrome

o

Would cause dry mouth + anti-Ro.

o

But psychosis, low C4, and anti-Smith positivity are not features.

Mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD)

o

Classic antibody is anti-U1 RNP, not anti-Smith.

o

Low complements are less prominent than in SLE.

o

Psychosis is not a major feature.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

Anti-Smith = SLE until proven otherwise.

•

Low complement = active SLE (especially renal/neuro).

•

Anti-Ro alone could suggest Sjögren's, but if anti-Smith is also
positive, SLE

is the diagnosis.

•

MCTD requires anti-U1 RNP as the hallmark.

stem: A 47-years-old man present with Raynaud's phenomenon Difficulty in swallowing. 8/10 Fingers has distorted capillary. What is the most appropriate treatment?

A 35-year-old man presented with an itchy rash on his arms and buttocks. 5 years ago, he was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes mellitus. On examination, he has multiple blisters on his forearms and buttock. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer

B. Dermatitis herpetiformis

Key Points from the Scenario

•

35-year-old man with T1DM → autoimmune background (high risk of other

autoimmune conditions).

•

Itchy rash + blisters on forearms and buttocks →

distribution is very typical.

•

Multiple blisters → vesiculobullous disorder.

•

Classic association = Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH), which is linked

with gluten-sensitive enteropathy (coeliac disease) and autoimmune

conditions like T1DM.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Dermatitis Herpetiformis)

•

Dermatitis herpetiformis is a chronic, intensely itchy blistering skin
condition.

•

Characteristic features:

o

Symmetrical pruritic vesicles/blisters on extensor surfaces (elbows,

forearms, knees, buttocks).

o

Caused by IgA deposition in dermal papillae.

o

Strong association with coeliac disease and other autoimmune

conditions (T1DM, thyroid disease).

•

Diagnosis: skin biopsy with granular IgA deposits (direct

immunofluorescence).

•

Treatment: Gluten-free diet + Dapsone (for skin lesions).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Candida albicans

o

Causes thrush (oral, genital) or intertrigo.

o

Not a blistering rash on extensor surfaces.

Dermatitis herpetiformis

o

Correct: pruritic, blistering rash on extensor surfaces in

T1DM/autoimmune context.

Necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum

o

Seen in diabetes.

o

Presents as yellow-brown atrophic plaques with telangiectasia on

shins.

o

Not itchy or blistering.

Sclerosis diabeticorum

o

Thickening/tightening of skin on upper back/neck in long-standing

diabetes.

o

Not blistering, not pruritic.

Erythema annulare multiforme

o

Target lesions (often after infections/drugs).

o

Not symmetrical blisters on extensor surfaces.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Dermatitis herpetiformis = itchy vesicles on extensor surfaces +

T1DM/coeliac link.

•

Necrobiosis lipoidica = yellow-brown plaques on shins.

•

Sclerosis diabeticorum = thick skin upper back/neck.

•

Candida = mucocutaneous infection, not blisters.

•

Erythema multiforme = target lesions, often post-infection.

stem: A 32-year-old woman was admitted with a history of paracetamol overdose. She reported that she would hear voices that would call her "pathetic & worthless", and she should take her life. She also mentioned that it started while she broke up with her girlfriend 3 months earlier. She made cuts in her arms to get rid of the voices. She has
options: history of cocaine use for socialisation. She also stated that her mood was all over the place. On examination, she has scars on her left forearm. Other physical examinations reveal no abnormality. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer

D. Depression with psychosis

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Young woman with paracetamol overdose → deliberate self-harm,

background of psychiatric illness.

•

Hears derogatory voices ("pathetic & worthless", "take your life") →

auditory hallucinations, mood-congruent with depression.

•

Started after breakup 3 months ago → stressor triggering depressive
episode.

•

Made cuts on arms → self-harm, strongly associated with depression and

suicidality.

•

Mood "all over the place" → emotional lability, but not classic for
mania.

•

No abnormal physical exam findings → ruling out acute delirium/medical

cause.

•

History of cocaine use → relevant, but presentation is chronic (3
months), not

acute intoxication/withdrawal.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Depression with Psychosis)

Depression with psychotic features = severe depressive disorder with

hallucinations or delusions.

•

Psychotic symptoms are typically mood-congruent (e.g., guilt,
worthlessness,

nihilism, voices telling them to die).

•

This case:

o

Suicidal ideation + overdose attempt.

o

Auditory hallucinations directly reinforcing depressive cognitions.

o

Duration = 3 months, not transient → rules out drug-induced.

•

Fits severe depressive episode with psychotic features.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Multiple personality disorder (dissociative identity disorder)

o

Characterised by two or more distinct identities.

o

Not described here --- this is psychosis with mood symptoms.

Schizophrenia

o

Requires ≥6 months with delusions, hallucinations, thought disorder,

negative symptoms.

o

Psychosis here is mood-congruent and occurs in depressive context →

not isolated schizophrenia.

Drug-induced psychosis

o

Cocaine can cause paranoia/hallucinations, but those are acute, linked
to

intoxication.

o

Here, symptoms persist for 3 months → not explained by cocaine alone.

Depression with psychosis

o

Fits best: depressive illness + self-harm + suicidal voices.

Mania / Bipolar disorder

o

Would present with elevated mood, grandiosity, decreased sleep,

pressured speech.

o

Not consistent with worthlessness + suicidal ideation.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Mood-congruent hallucinations/delusions = psychotic depression.

•

Mood-incongruent psychosis (e.g., grandiose delusions in depression) →

think schizoaffective.

•

Drug-induced psychosis → acute, short-lived, temporally related to
substance.

•

Schizophrenia → chronic, psychosis independent of mood.

stem: Ulcer found on endoscopy Blood supply to the posterior duodenal cap?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Gastroduodenal artery

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Ulcer in the posterior duodenal cap (first part of duodenum).

•

Posterior duodenal ulcers are notorious for severe bleeding.

•

The vessel most often eroded = gastroduodenal artery.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Gastroduodenal artery)

•

The first part of the duodenum (duodenal bulb/cap) lies close to
several

major vessels:

Thiazides → hyponatraemia + gout.

•

Spironolactone → gynaecomastia.

•

Statins → check CK & LFTs if symptomatic.

Mnemonic for ACEi adverse effects: "CATCHH"

•

Cough

•

Angioedema

•

Teratogenic

•

Creatinine ↑ (renal impairment)

•

Hyperkalaemia

•

Hypotension (first-dose effect)

stem: Pt had a history of Sweating, colonic polyps, thyroid goitre, daytime somnolence, axillary tags, bilateral CTS, HTN, T2DM Which test will help to make the diagnosis?
options: OGTT for GH suppression (gold standard for acromegaly)
explanation:
Correct Answer

B. OGTT for GH (Oral Glucose Tolerance Test for Growth Hormone
suppression)

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Multiple systemic features given:

o

Sweating → hyperhidrosis (autonomic symptom).

Anterior ulcer → risk of perforation into peritoneum.

o

Posterior ulcer → risk of bleeding due to erosion of

the gastroduodenal artery.

•

Gastroduodenal artery is a branch of the common hepatic artery (from the

•

This is a high-yield exam fact: posterior duodenal ulcer bleeding =

gastroduodenal artery erosion.

2\. Splenic artery

o

Runs along the superior border of the pancreas.

o

Eroded by posterior gastric ulcers, not duodenal ones.

3\. Duodenal artery

o

Not a standard named vessel in this context.

o

Exam distractor.

•

Posterior duodenal ulcer → bleeding from gastroduodenal artery.

•

Anterior duodenal ulcer → perforation.

•

Posterior gastric ulcer → bleeding from splenic artery.
