stem: A pt presented with cystic fibrosis & 6 months history of loose offensive stool, stunted growth and 5 kg weight loss On examination, no significant abnormality except short stature Investigation for diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer

D. Faecal elastase

Key Points from the Scenario

Cystic fibrosis patient → high risk of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency
(EPI).

•

Loose, offensive stool (steatorrhoea) + stunted growth + weight loss →

classic features of fat malabsorption.

•

No other abnormal exam findings except short stature → chronic

malabsorption rather than acute inflammation.

•

The question is asking for the best diagnostic investigation for
pancreatic

exocrine insufficiency in CF.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Faecal Elastase)

•

Faecal elastase is a non-invasive stool test used to assess pancreatic
exocrine

function.

•

Low faecal elastase = pancreatic insufficiency.

•

In CF, pancreatic enzyme deficiency → failure to digest fats →
steatorrhoea,

malnutrition, poor growth.

•

This is the gold standard initial test in suspected exocrine pancreatic

insufficiency.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Faecal calprotectin

o

Marker of intestinal inflammation (e.g., IBD).

o

Not a test for pancreatic insufficiency.

Hydrogen breath test

o

Used for lactose intolerance or small intestinal bacterial overgrowth

(SIBO).

o

Not relevant here.

Duodenal biopsy

o

Used to diagnose coeliac disease.

o

Not first-line in CF patient with clear steatorrhoea picture.

Faecal elastase

o

Correct: best diagnostic test for pancreatic exocrine insufficiency in

CF.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

CF + steatorrhoea/poor growth = pancreatic insufficiency → test with

faecal elastase.

•

Faecal calprotectin = IBD.

Hydrogen breath = lactose intolerance/SIBO.

•

Duodenal biopsy = coeliac disease.

stem: A 45-years-old woman presents with 9 months H/O burping. No H/O vomiting. H/O duodenal ulcer with H. pylori eradication. Other examinations were normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer

A. Aerophagia

Key Points from the Scenario

•

45-year-old woman with 9 months of burping → isolated, chronic symptom.

•

No vomiting → rules out gastric outlet obstruction (GOO).

•

Past H. pylori & duodenal ulcer (eradicated) → not currently symptomatic

(no pain, no ulcer recurrence signs).

•

Other examinations normal → no red flag features (no dysphagia, weight
loss,

haematemesis).

Burping alone is usually due to swallowing excess air (aerophagia)
rather

than structural GI disease.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Aerophagia)

•

Aerophagia = repetitive swallowing of air,

leading to belching/burping.

•

Common in anxiety, habit, or functional dyspepsia.

•

It presents with isolated burping without vomiting, weight loss, or
dysphagia.

•

In this case, since all other findings are normal, the most likely
explanation

is functional aerophagia.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Aerophagia

o

Correct → most likely in isolated burping with normal exam.

Gastric Outlet Obstruction (GOO)

o

Causes persistent vomiting, early satiety,

abdominal distension.

o

Not present here.

H. pylori Gastritis

o

Would cause dyspepsia, epigastric pain, nausea.

o

Patient already treated, no such symptoms now.

Hiatus Hernia

o

Causes reflux, regurgitation, chest discomfort.

o

Not just burping.

Pharyngeal Pouch (Zenker's diverticulum)

o

Causes dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested

food, halitosis, gurgling in

neck.

o

Not isolated burping.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Isolated burping → think Aerophagia (functional).

•

GOO → vomiting + distension.

•

Hiatus hernia → reflux/regurgitation.

•

Pharyngeal pouch → dysphagia + regurgitation.

•

H. pylori gastritis → pain/dyspepsia.

ANSWERS:

Subcutaneous insulin

Correct Answer

A. Subcutaneous insulin

Key Points from the Scenario

•

19-year-old with 2 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss → classic

presentation of new-onset diabetes mellitus.

•

BMI 22.5 → not obese → points towards Type 1 diabetes mellitus

(T1DM) rather than Type 2.

•

Glucose 14.2 mmol/L → hyperglycaemia but not extreme.

•

Ketones normal, bicarbonate normal → so not DKA.

•

Stable patient with T1DM diagnosis → treatment = subcutaneous

insulin (lifelong).

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Subcutaneous Insulin)

•

T1DM results from autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β-cells →
absolute

insulin deficiency.

•

Patients are usually young, lean, with rapid onset symptoms (polyuria,

polydipsia, weight loss).

•

Even in the absence of DKA, insulin is always required.

•

Management here: start subcutaneous insulin regimen (basal-bolus or

twice-daily regimen).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Subcutaneous insulin

o

Correct choice for new-onset T1DM without DKA.

Metformin

o

First-line for T2DM in overweight patients.

o

Not appropriate in this lean, young patient with T1DM.

Diet and Lifestyle

o

May help in impaired glucose tolerance or early T2DM.

o

Not sufficient in T1DM (absolute insulin deficiency).

Gliclazide

o

Sulfonylurea; stimulates insulin release from β-cells.

o

Ineffective in T1DM (no functioning β-cells).

IV fixed-rate insulin

o

Indicated in DKA or HHS.

o

This patient has normal bicarbonate & ketones, so no need for IV

insulin.

•

Young, lean, rapid onset symptoms → Type 1 DM → Subcutaneous insulin.

Hydration, MODY → Mild (Sulfonylurea)"

stem: A 41 years-old with T2DM, CKD stage 4 H/O 8 weeks pregnant on Gliclazide. What is the next step in management?
explanation:
Correct Answer

A. Change gliclazide to insulin

Key Points from the Scenario

•

41-year-old with T2DM, CKD stage 4 → advanced CKD, reduced renal

clearance.

•

8 weeks pregnant → special considerations (avoid teratogenic or unsafe

drugs).

•

Currently on gliclazide (sulfonylurea).

•

Sulfonylureas cross the placenta → risk of

neonatal hypoglycaemia.

•

Metformin is used in some pregnancies, but contraindicated in advanced

CKD (eGFR \<30, stage 4/5) due to risk of lactic acidosis.

•

Therefore, the safest choice is insulin.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Change to Insulin)

•

In pregnancy with diabetes (T1DM, T2DM, or new GDM), insulin is the

treatment of choice because:

o

Does not cross placenta.

o

Safest and most effective for strict glycaemic control.

•

In CKD stage 4, oral agents are limited:

o

Metformin contraindicated (risk lactic acidosis).

o

Sulfonylureas (like gliclazide) cross placenta, unsafe in pregnancy.

•

Hence → switch to insulin for both pregnancy and CKD safety.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Change gliclazide to insulin

Correct → safest option in pregnancy with advanced CKD.

2\. Change to metformin

o

Metformin is often used in pregnancy (esp. GDM, PCOS).

o

BUT contraindicated in CKD stage 4 (risk lactic

acidosis).

3\. Keep on gliclazide

o

Unsafe → crosses placenta, can cause neonatal hypoglycaemia.

o

Not recommended in pregnancy.

High-Yield Exam Takeaway

•

Pregnancy + T1DM or T2DM → Insulin = gold standard.

•

Metformin: safe in pregnancy, but contraindicated in CKD stage 4/5.

•

Sulfonylureas: cross placenta → avoid.

stem: An 87-years-old man. H/O LUTS. Which one will decrease the size of prostate?
explanation:
Correct Answer

A. Finasteride

Key Points from the Scenario

•

87-year-old man with LUTS (Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms) → most likely

due to benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).

•

Question asks: which drug decreases the size of the prostate.

•

Different LUTS drugs:

o

α-blockers (e.g., tamsulosin, indoramin) → relax smooth muscle →

improve flow, but do not shrink prostate.

o

5α-reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) → block conversion

of testosterone to DHT → reduce prostate volume

Antimuscarinics (tolterodine) → used for overactive bladder

symptoms, not for prostate size.

o

Cyproterone acetate → anti-androgen, not used in routine BPH (used in

prostate cancer, paraphilia).

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Finasteride)

•

Finasteride is a 5α-reductase inhibitor.

•

Mechanism: prevents conversion of testosterone → dihydrotestosterone
(DHT),

the main androgen responsible for prostate growth.

•

Effects:

o

Reduces prostate size by \~20--30% over months.

o

Improves symptoms and reduces risk of urinary retention.

o

Takes several months to work (slower than α-blockers).

•

Used especially in larger prostates (\>40 ml).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Finasteride

o

Correct: only option here that truly reduces prostate size.

Cyproterone acetate

o

Anti-androgen used in prostate cancer, hypersexuality, paraphilia.

o

Not used for BPH routinely.

Indoramin

o

α1-blocker → relaxes bladder neck/prostatic smooth muscle.

o

Improves symptoms, but does not shrink prostate.

Tamsulosin

o

Selective α1A-blocker → relieves LUTS quickly.

o

No effect on prostate size.

Tolterodine

o

Antimuscarinic → used for overactive bladder/urge incontinence.

o

Not for prostate shrinkage.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

α-blockers (tamsulosin, indoramin) = rapid symptom relief, no effect
on size.

•

5α-reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) = shrink prostate,
long-

term benefit.

•

Antimuscarinics (tolterodine) = OAB, not BPH size.

Anti-androgens (cyproterone, flutamide) = prostate cancer, not LUTS.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

•

•

•

Mnemonic for exams:

•

"FAST"

o

Alpha-blocker = Act fast (symptom relief).

o

Stolterodine (Tolterodine) = Storage/OAB symptoms.

o

Tadalafil = Two-in-one (LUTS + ED).

BPH Management Algorithm

Step 1: Initial assessment

•

LUTS severity (IPSS score, symptom impact).

•

Rule out red flags: haematuria, recurrent UTIs, retention, renal
impairment

→ refer urology.

Step 2: Lifestyle & Conservative Measures (Mild symptoms)

•

Fluid restriction in evening

•

Reduce caffeine & alcohol

•

Bladder training

➡ If symptoms controlled → continue conservative.

➡ If persistent / moderate--severe → go to Step 3.

Step 3: Pharmacological Management (Moderate--Severe LUTS)

👉 Voiding (obstructive) symptoms predominant

•

α1-blocker (Tamsulosin / Alfuzosin) → rapid

relief (days--weeks)

•

If large prostate (\>40ml) or PSA high → add 5α-reductase inhibitor

(Finasteride / Dutasteride) for shrinkage

👉 Storage (irritative/OAB) symptoms predominant

•

Antimuscarinic (Tolterodine, Solifenacin)

•

Or β3-agonist (Mirabegron) if antimuscarinic contraindicated

👉 LUTS + Erectile Dysfunction

•

Consider PDE-5 inhibitor (Tadalafil)

Step 4: Combination Therapy

•

α-blocker + 5α-reductase inhibitor if severe LUTS and large prostate

•

Improves symptoms + prevents progression

Step 5: Surgical / Minimally Invasive (if refractory / complications)

•

TURP (Transurethral Resection of Prostate)

•

HoLEP, UroLift, Open prostatectomy (for very large glands)

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Only Finasteride/Dutasteride shrink prostate.

•

Tamsulosin = rapid relief, no shrinkage.

•

Tolterodine = OAB/storage symptoms.

•

Tadalafil = LUTS + ED.

•

Surgery = retention, hydronephrosis, recurrent UTIs, failure of medical

therapy.

Mnemonic: "FAST Track BPH"

•

Finasteride = Shrink size

•

Alpha-blocker = Fast relief

•

Stolterodine (Tolterodine) = Storage symptoms

•

Tadalafil = Two-in-one (ED + LUTS)

stem: A 52 year old Nigerian man has a history of hypertension, T2DM, ischaemic heart disease. For these conditions he is taking atorvastatin, gliclazide, indapamide, metformin, ramipril. For the last few days, he has been complaining of swelling of tongue. Which of the following drugs is most probable related to his angioedema?
explanation:
Correct Answer

E. Ramipril

Key Points from the Scenario

•

52-year-old Nigerian man with multiple comorbidities (HTN, T2DM, IHD).

•

Swelling of tongue (angioedema) → classic side effect clue.

•

Medications: atorvastatin, gliclazide, indapamide, metformin, ramipril.

•

ACE inhibitors (ramipril) → cause bradykinin-

mediated angioedema, more

common in patients of African descent.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Ramipril)

•

ACE inhibitor--induced angioedema occurs in \~0.1--0.7% of patients.

•

Pathophysiology: ACE normally breaks down bradykinin. ACE inhibition → ↑

bradykinin → ↑ vascular permeability → swelling of lips, tongue, face,
larynx.

•

Can occur any time during treatment (days to years after starting).

•

More common in:

o

African descent

o

Women

o

Smokers

•

Life-threatening risk = airway compromise.

•

Management: stop ACE inhibitor immediately, supportive therapy; switch
to

ARB if needed (much lower risk).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Atorvastatin

o

Common SE: myopathy, liver enzyme rise.

o

Not angioedema.

Gliclazide (sulfonylurea)

o

SE: hypoglycaemia, weight gain.

o

No link to angioedema.

Indapamide (thiazide-like diuretic)

o

SE: hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, hypercalcaemia.

o

Not angioedema.

Metformin

o

SE: GI upset, lactic acidosis (rare).

o

No angioedema association.

Ramipril

o

Classic cause of ACE inhibitor--induced angioedema.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

ACE inhibitors (e.g., Ramipril, Lisinopril) → angioedema (bradykinin

mediated).

•

More common in African/Caribbean patients.

•

Management = stop ACE inhibitor immediately.

•

Do not rechallenge with another ACE inhibitor. Consider ARB if
alternative

needed.

ACEi → angioedema (stop immediately, don't rechallenge).

•

stem: Pt had a history of Sweating, colonic polyps, thyroid goitre, daytime somnolence, axillary tags, bilateral CTS, HTN, T2DM Which test will help to make the diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer

B. OGTT for GH (Oral Glucose Tolerance Test for Growth Hormone
suppression)

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Multiple systemic features given:

o

Sweating → hyperhidrosis (autonomic symptom).

Colonic polyps → increased risk in acromegaly.

o

Thyroid goitre → common association with acromegaly.

o

Daytime somnolence → obstructive sleep apnoea from soft tissue

overgrowth.

o

Axillary skin tags → metabolic association, also seen in acromegaly.

o

Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome → classic complication of acromegaly

due to soft tissue swelling.

o

HTN + T2DM → strongly associated with acromegaly.

•

All point towards acromegaly.

•

Diagnostic test: failure of GH suppression after oral glucose tolerance
test

(OGTT) is confirmatory.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (OGTT for GH suppression)

•

In healthy individuals: oral glucose load suppresses GH.

•

In acromegaly: GH secretion is autonomous → no suppression (sometimes

paradoxical rise).

•

Therefore, OGTT for GH suppression = diagnostic

gold standard.

•

Additional tests:

o

IGF-1 (screening test, elevated in acromegaly).

o

Pituitary MRI (to identify GH-secreting adenoma).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Plasma catecholamines

o

Used to diagnose pheochromocytoma.

o

Symptoms would be paroxysmal headache, palpitations, sweating, labile

BP.

o

Not the systemic picture here.

OGTT for GH suppression

o

Correct diagnostic test for acromegaly.

Cortisol

o

Used in suspected Cushing's syndrome (screening with overnight

dexamethasone suppression).

o

No Cushingoid features described here.

Acromegaly features: acral enlargement, sweating, OSA, colonic polyps,

thyroid goitre, carpal tunnel, HTN, DM.

•

Best screening = IGF-1.

•

Confirmatory test = OGTT for GH suppression.

stem: A 25-years-old woman. Sister has endometrial Ca. Father has Colon Ca. Paternal uncle has Rectal Ca. Dx?
explanation:
Correct Answer

A. Lynch syndrome (Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer, HNPCC)

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Strong family history of colorectal cancers (colon + rectal cancer in
close

relatives).

•

Endometrial cancer in sister → classic extra-colonic tumour linked to
Lynch

syndrome.

•

Age 25 → young patient, family pattern strongly suggests inherited
cancer

syndrome.

•

No mention of hundreds of polyps → rules out FAP.

•

No mucocutaneous pigmentation, breast/thyroid lesions, or

hamartomas → rules out PJS and Cowden.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Lynch Syndrome)

•

Lynch syndrome = Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC).

•

Cause: Germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes (MLH1,

MSH2, MSH6, PMS2).

•

Cancers associated:

o

Colorectal (proximal colon common)

o

Endometrial (most common extracolonic tumour)

o

Ovarian, gastric, urinary tract, biliary tract, small bowel.

•

Clues in exam: multiple family members, young onset, CRC + endometrial

cancer.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Lynch syndrome (HNPCC)

o

Correct: colon + rectal + endometrial cancer in family.

Cowden syndrome

o

Associated with PTEN mutation.

o

Causes breast, thyroid (follicular), endometrial

cancers,

mucocutaneous lesions.

o

But strong colorectal clustering not typical.

FAP (Familial Adenomatous Polyposis)

o

Hundreds to thousands of adenomatous polyps → CRC by age 40 if

untreated.

o

Not described here.

Juvenile polyposis

o

Hamartomatous polyps in colon/stomach, presents with

bleeding/anemia in childhood.

o

Not this presentation.

Peutz--Jeghers syndrome (PJS)

o

Hamartomatous polyps + mucocutaneous pigmentation (lips, buccal

mucosa, fingers).

o

Increased risk of GI and pancreatic cancers.

o

No pigmentation mentioned.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

CRC + endometrial Ca in family = Lynch syndrome.

Hundreds of adenomatous polyps = FAP.

•

Hamartomatous polyps + pigmented lips = PJS.

•

Hamartomatous polyps + bleeding in childhood = Juvenile polyposis.

•

Breast + thyroid + endometrial + mucocutaneous lesions = Cowden.

stem: An 18-years-old presents with 2 years H/O MSK pain, JTs, Early morning stiffness. Has scalp Psoriasis & O/E showed synovitis, Scaling of psoriasis, increase Skin laxity, stretch mark of thigh. Which assessment / scoring will you do?
explanation:
Correct Answer

C. DAS 28 (Disease Activity Score in 28 joints)

Key Points from the Scenario

•

18-year-old with 2 years MSK pain, early morning stiffness, and

synovitis → strongly suggests inflammatory arthritis.

•

History of scalp psoriasis → points to psoriatic arthritis.

•

Exam findings: synovitis + psoriasis skin lesions.

•

The key question: which scoring system is most appropriate to assess
disease

activity in inflammatory arthritis?

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (DAS 28)

DAS 28 (Disease Activity Score -- 28 joints) is used to assess disease
activity

in inflammatory arthritis, including psoriatic arthritis.

•

It involves:

o

Tender joint count (28 joints)

o

Swollen joint count (28 joints)

o

ESR/CRP

o

Patient's global assessment of health

•

Helps guide escalation of therapy (DMARDs/biologics).

•

Although CASPAR criteria are used to diagnose PsA, DAS 28 is used

for monitoring arthritis severity.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Psoriatic Arthritis Severity Index

o

This is not a standard validated score for arthritis activity.

o

Likely a distractor.

Beighton Laxity Score

o

Used for joint hypermobility / Ehlers-Danlos / Marfan.

o

Not relevant here (inflammatory arthritis).

DAS 28

o

Correct → assesses disease activity in inflammatory arthritis (RA,
PsA).

PASI (Psoriasis Area and Severity Index)

o

Used to assess severity of skin psoriasis, not arthritis.

Schober Test

o

Used to assess lumbar spine flexibility in ankylosing spondylitis.

o

Not relevant here.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

DAS 28 → disease activity in inflammatory arthritis (RA, PsA).

•

PASI → severity of skin psoriasis.

•

Beighton → hypermobility.

•

Schober → lumbar spine stiffness (AS).

•

CASPAR criteria → diagnosis of psoriatic arthritis (but not asked
here).

stem: A 45 year old male presented with 6 months history of hair loss, sore patch on scalp and face. O/E: focal patches of scarring alopecia, erythema, and follicular plugging. Dx?
explanation:
Correct Answer

C. Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE)

Key Points from the Scenario

•

45-year-old man with 6 months of hair loss +

sore scalp patches.

•

Exam findings:

o

Focal patches of scarring alopecia → hallmark of DLE.

o

Erythema + follicular plugging → very characteristic of DLE lesions.

•

Other options considered, but DLE fits best with this triad: scarring
alopecia +

erythema + follicular plugging.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Discoid Lupus Erythematosus)

•

DLE = chronic cutaneous form of lupus erythematosus.

Clinical features:

o

Sharply demarcated erythematous plaques.

o

Follicular plugging with scaling.

o

Central atrophy and scarring → leads to irreversible alopecia.

o

Sun-exposed areas commonly affected (scalp, face, ears).

•

Important as 10--20% may progress to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

•

Diagnosis: skin biopsy (interface dermatitis, basement membrane
thickening,

perivascular infiltrates).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Chronic plaque psoriasis

o

Causes silvery scales on erythematous plaques.

o

Alopecia is non-scarring, unlike here.

o

Follicular plugging not seen.

Cutaneous sarcoidosis

o

Can cause plaques/nodules, but scarring alopecia + follicular

plugging not typical.

o

Would expect papules/nodules, often reddish-brown.

Discoid lupus erythematosus

o

Fits perfectly: scarring alopecia + erythema + follicular plugging.

Discoid eczema

o

Causes coin-shaped eczematous lesions, pruritic.

o

No follicular plugging, no scarring alopecia.

Lichen planus (lichen planopilaris)

o

Can cause scarring alopecia, but lesions are violaceous, flat-topped

papules.

o

No follicular plugging.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Scarring alopecia + follicular plugging + erythematous plaques on

scalp/face = Discoid Lupus Erythematosus (DLE).

•

Non-scarring alopecia → Psoriasis, Eczema.

•

Violaceous papules → Lichen planus.

•

Nodular reddish plaques → Sarcoidosis.

stem: Pregnant lady of 12 weeks comes in with 3 weeks H/O fatigue. Her TSH is low and FT4 & FT3 within normal range, was low. Her anti-TPO ab is positive. What is the most likely underlying cause?
explanation:
Correct Answer

B. Pregnancy

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Pregnant woman, 12 weeks → 1st trimester.

•

TSH is low.

•

FT4 and FT3 are normal (not raised).

•

Anti-TPO positive → autoimmune thyroiditis background, but not the
direct

cause of current low TSH.

•

In early pregnancy, hCG is structurally similar to TSH and can weakly

stimulate TSH receptors.

•

This causes a physiological fall in TSH during the 1st trimester, with
normal

FT4/FT3 (sometimes high-normal).

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Pregnancy effect)

•

In the 1st trimester, high hCG levels (peak around 8--12 weeks) → mild

stimulation of thyroid → mild suppression of TSH.

•

FT4 and FT3 usually remain in the normal or upper-normal range.

•

This phenomenon is gestational transient thyrotoxicosis or physiological

suppression of TSH in pregnancy.

•

No treatment needed if FT4/FT3 normal and patient asymptomatic.

•

Anti-TPO positivity suggests higher risk of developing postpartum

thyroiditis or hypothyroidism later, but not the

cause of low TSH here.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Levothyroxine use

o

Would show suppressed TSH + high FT4 (not normal).

o

No history of hypothyroidism given.

2\. Pregnancy

o

Correct: explains low TSH with normal FT4/FT3 in 1st trimester.

3\. Thyrotoxicosis / Thyroiditis

o

Would show low TSH + elevated FT4/FT3, sometimes painful gland.

o

Here FT4/FT3 are normal.

4\. Thyroid nodule (toxic nodule)

o

Causes suppressed TSH + elevated thyroid hormones.

o

Not consistent with normal FT4/FT3.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Early pregnancy → low TSH, normal FT4/FT3 (physiological, hCG-driven).

•

Anti-TPO positive → risk of thyroid dysfunction later, but not the cause
here.

•

Thyrotoxicosis / toxic nodule → would raise FT4/FT3.

•

Levothyroxine therapy → TSH suppressed, FT4 high.

Correct Answer

A. Sick Euthyroid Syndrome

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Patient with acute exacerbation of COPD (severe intercurrent illness).

•

TSH = 0.2 (slightly low)

•

FT4 = 12 (normal--low)

•

FT3 = 1.5 (low)

Anti-TPO = 70 (positive but may be incidental, not the cause of current

picture).

•

This pattern = low T3, normal/low T4, low/normal TSH → classic for Sick

Euthyroid Syndrome (Non-Thyroidal Illness Syndrome).

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Sick Euthyroid Syndrome)

•

Occurs in critically ill or hospitalized patients.

•

Pathophysiology:

o

↓ peripheral conversion of T4 → T3.

o

↑ reverse T3.

o

TSH may be low, normal, or slightly elevated.

•

Pattern:

o

Low T3 (hallmark)

o

Normal or low T4

o

TSH low/normal

•

Important: Do NOT treat with thyroxine; it corrects once the acute
illness

resolves.

Sick euthyroid syndrome

o

Fits perfectly: acute illness + low T3, low/normal T4, low TSH.

o

Would show ↑ TSH + ↓ T4.

o

Here TSH is low, not high.

Secondary hypothyroidism (pituitary)

o

Would show low/normal TSH + low T4, but FT3 not selectively low.

o

Also, no acute illness context usually.

Thyroid hormone resistance

o

Would show normal/high TSH + high T4/T3.

o

Not the case here.

Thyroiditis

o

Usually has biphasic pattern: thyrotoxic (↑T4, ↓TSH) → hypothyroid

(↑TSH, ↓T4).

o

Not matching this profile.

Acute illness setting

A 67 year old Female diagnosed with RA coming up with a 6 month H/O
swelling on

the olecranon, which was diagnosed as Rheumatoid Nodule.

What is the predominant Cell type in a rheumatoid nodule?

Basophils

Eosinophils

Macrophages

Natural Killer Cells

Neutrophils

ANSWERS:

Macrophages

Correct Answer

Macrophages

Key Points from the Scenario

•

67-year-old woman with RA → common extra-articular finding is
rheumatoid

nodule, especially at pressure points (olecranon).

•

Rheumatoid nodules = granulomatous inflammation.

•

Histology shows:

o

Central area of fibrinoid necrosis.

o

Surrounded by palisading macrophages/epithelioid cells.

o

Outer zone of lymphocytes and plasma cells.

•

Therefore, the predominant cell type = macrophages.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Macrophages)

•

In rheumatoid nodules:

o

Centre: fibrinoid necrosis (immune complex deposition).

o

Middle zone: palisading macrophages (epithelioid histiocytes).

Outer zone: chronic inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes, plasma cells).

•

Macrophages = key in forming granulomas and sustaining inflammation in
RA.

•

This structure resembles a granuloma; hence

macrophages are the hallmark.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Basophils

o

Role in allergic reactions, histamine release.

o

Not seen in RA nodules.

Eosinophils

o

Associated with allergy, parasitic infection, Churg--Strauss.

o

Not relevant to rheumatoid nodules.

Macrophages

o

Correct: palisading arrangement around necrotic centre in rheumatoid

nodules.

Natural Killer Cells

o

Part of innate immunity, antiviral/tumour defence.

o

Not a feature of granulomatous inflammation.

Neutrophils

o

Present in acute inflammation and pus formation.

o

Nodules are chronic granulomatous lesions, not neutrophil-rich

abscesses.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Rheumatoid nodules = central fibrinoid necrosis + palisading

macrophages (epithelioid histiocytes).

•

Classic extra-articular feature of RA, especially in seropositive
disease.

stem: A lady with recent diagnosis of diabetes had a traumatic below-knee amputation 4 months ago. Which serum marker best reflects glycaemic control over the past 3 months?
SSC of Lung + Hyper Ca presented with polyuria & polydipsia What is the initial treatment of choice?
explanation:
Correct Answer

A\) Normal Saline

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Patient with squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the lung.

•

Presents with polyuria & polydipsia → classic features of hypercalcaemia
(due

to PTHrP secretion in SCC).

•

Question is about the initial treatment.

•

First step in severe hypercalcaemia = aggressive IV hydration with
normal

saline.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Normal Saline)

•

Hypercalcaemia causes dehydration (polyuria via nephrogenic DI-like
effect,

vomiting, anorexia).

•

Normal saline IV rehydration:

o

Restores intravascular volume.

o

Enhances renal calcium excretion.

•

Only after adequate rehydration, additional measures can be considered:

o

IV bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid, pamidronate) → longer-term

calcium control.

o

Calcitonin (short-term, rapid onset but less sustained).

o

Loop diuretics (frusemide) → only after rehydration to promote

calciuresis.

•

Therefore, the first-line immediate management = IV normal saline.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Normal Saline

o

Correct: initial step in managing hypercalcaemia.

Thiazide

o

Worsens hypercalcaemia (reduces renal calcium excretion).

Contraindicated.

Dexamethasone

o

Used in hypercalcaemia due to lymphoma or vitamin D--mediated

causes.

o

Not first-line here.

Frusemide (Loop diuretic)

o

Promotes calciuresis, but only after adequate IV hydration.

o

Giving it early worsens dehydration and renal function.

Zoledronic Acid (Bisphosphonate)

o

Very effective in malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia.

o

But onset is delayed (2--4 days) → not initial treatment.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (esp. SCC lung) → PTHrP secretion.

•

Step 1 = IV normal saline hydration.

•

Step 2 = Bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid).

•

Loop diuretics only after rehydration.

•

Steroids for lymphoma/vitamin D--driven hypercalcaemia.

Hypercalcaemia Management: Stepwise Approach

Step 1: Initial Treatment (Immediate Stabilisation)

•

IV Normal Saline (0.9% NaCl) 💧

o

First-line in all severe hypercalcaemia.

o

Restores intravascular volume (patients are dehydrated due to

polyuria/vomiting).

o

Enhances renal calcium excretion.

Step 2: Promote Calciuresis (After Rehydration)

•

IV Loop Diuretic (Furosemide/Frusemide)

o

Only after rehydration.

o

Increases urinary calcium excretion.

o

Monitor K⁺ & Mg²⁺ (risk of hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia).

Step 3: Treat Underlying Cause (Definitive Control)

IV Bisphosphonates (Zoledronic acid, Pamidronate) 🦴

o

Inhibit osteoclast activity.

o

Very effective in malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia.

o

Onset: 2--4 days (not immediate).

Step 4: Adjuncts (Depending on Aetiology)

•

Calcitonin (fast-acting, temporary effect).

•

Glucocorticoids (e.g., dexamethasone) → for lymphoma, vitamin
D--mediated

hypercalcaemia (e.g., sarcoidosis).

•

Dialysis → if refractory or in renal failure.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

SCC of lung → PTHrP → hypercalcaemia.

•

Initial = IV normal saline.

•

Bisphosphonates = main long-term treatment (esp. malignancy).

•

Steroids = for vitamin D--driven causes

(lymphoma, sarcoid).

•

Thiazides are contraindicated (worsen hypercalcaemia).

Mnemonic: "Hydrate → Loop → Block Bone → Special Cause"

Hydrate (normal saline)

Loop diuretic (after hydration)

Block bone resorption (bisphosphonate)

Special cause treatment (steroid/dialysis)

stem: A 54 yr old chronic alcoholic presented with abdominal distention, discomfort, malaise. OE showed distended and tender abdomen, Pitting oedema on both limbs. What is the best step in investigation to help in management?
explanation:
Correct Answer

B\) Ascitic fluid microscopy

Key Points from the Scenario

•

54-year-old chronic alcoholic → likely cirrhosis with ascites.

•

Presents with abdominal distention, malaise, mild tenderness → raises

suspicion for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP).

•

In suspected SBP, the most useful first-line test to guide management is

diagnostic paracentesis with ascitic fluid analysis.

•

Cell count (microscopy, especially neutrophils/PMN count) is the most

important, as:

o

PMN ≥250/mm³ = diagnostic for SBP, even if culture negative.

•

Culture is helpful, but it takes time and may be negative in many cases.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Ascitic fluid microscopy)

•

SBP = infection of ascitic fluid without secondary source.

•

Diagnosis:

o

PMN count ≥250 cells/mm³ (neutrophils on microscopy) = diagnostic.

o

Ascitic fluid culture confirms, but is less sensitive and slower.

•

Early diagnosis is critical because mortality is high if untreated.

•

Management: IV antibiotics (e.g., cefotaxime or ceftriaxone) + albumin
in

selected patients.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Ascitic fluid culture

o

Useful, but less sensitive (may be negative in up to 60%).

o

Takes time; does not guide immediate management.

Ascitic fluid microscopy

Correct: quickest and most sensitive test for diagnosing SBP (PMN ≥250

cells/mm³).

3\. Blood cultures

o

May show bacteraemia but are not diagnostic for SBP.

4\. Ultrasound Abdomen (USS)

o

Good for detecting ascites, cirrhosis, or focal lesions.

o

Does not confirm infection.

5\. CT Abdomen

o

Useful for complications (abscess, perforation), not for initial
diagnosis of

SBP.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Any cirrhotic patient with ascites + abdominal pain/tenderness/malaise →

do ascitic tap.

•

Diagnosis of SBP = PMN ≥250/mm³ on ascitic fluid microscopy.

•

Culture is supportive, not diagnostic.

stem: Bronchial asthma history, severe for 3 days, patient can't talk full sentence, tachycardiac, BP normal. Blood PH normal, HCO3 normal, CO2 low normal? On oxygen. Salbutamol nebulisation given every 15 min, ipratropium also ongoing & prednisolone given. Next best step in management?
explanation:
Correct Answer

C\) IV Magnesium Sulphate

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Severe asthma attack:

o

Can't complete sentences

Tachycardia

o

Normal BP

o

ABG: pH normal, HCO₃⁻ normal, CO₂ low-normal → patient

is hyperventilating (still compensating, not yet life-threatening).

•

Already given:

o

Oxygen

o

Frequent nebulised salbutamol

o

Ipratropium bromide

o

Oral prednisolone

•

Question: what is the next escalation step?

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (IV Magnesium Sulphate)

•

IV MgSO₄ is recommended in acute severe asthma not responding to initial

inhaled bronchodilators + steroids.

•

It works as a bronchodilator by inhibiting smooth muscle contraction and

reducing histamine release.

•

It is the next step before IV β-agonists or aminophylline.

•

Evidence shows it improves airflow and reduces hospital admissions in
severe

attacks.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

IV Salbutamol

o

Used only if asthma is life-threatening or unresponsive to nebulised

therapy + MgSO₄.

o

Not the immediate next step.

IV Theophylline (Aminophylline)

o

Rarely used now due to limited benefit + significant side effects.

o

Not the next step in acute severe asthma.

IV Magnesium Sulphate

o

Correct: next escalation after oxygen + nebs + steroids in severe
asthma.

IV Hydrocortisone

o

Steroids already given (oral prednisolone).

o

Oral is equally effective unless patient is vomiting/unable to
swallow.

Salmeterol (long-acting β₂ agonist, LABA)

o

Never used in acute setting.

o

Maintenance therapy only.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

Severe acute asthma (unable to talk, tachycardia, low-normal PaCO₂,
still

compensating) →

o

Oxygen + nebs (salbutamol/ipratropium) + steroids = first-line.

o

Next = IV MgSO₄.

o

If deteriorates further → consider IV salbutamol or aminophylline + ITU

referral.

Acute Asthma: Stepwise Management & ABG Patterns

Moderate Asthma

•

Clinical: Able to talk in full sentences, PEF \>50--75% predicted, RR
\<25, HR

\<110.

•

ABG: Normal.

•

Treatment:

o

Oxygen (target sats 94--98%)

o

Nebulised salbutamol ± ipratropium

o

Oral prednisolone

Severe Asthma

•

Clinical: Can't complete sentences, RR ≥25, HR ≥110, PEF 33--50%.

•

ABG: pH normal, HCO₃⁻ normal, PaCO₂ low/low-normal (due to

hyperventilation).

•

Treatment:

o

Oxygen + nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium

o

Oral/IV steroids

o

IV magnesium sulphate (next escalation if poor response)

Life-Threatening Asthma

•

Clinical: Silent chest, cyanosis, poor respiratory effort, arrhythmia,
exhaustion,

hypotension, PEF \<33%.

•

ABG: Normal or high PaCO₂, hypoxaemia,

acidosis (pH \<7.35) → indicates

tiring.

•

Treatment:

o

High-flow oxygen

o

Nebulised salbutamol/ipratropium

o

IV steroids

o

Consider IV salbutamol or IV aminophylline

o

Urgent ITU referral, prepare for intubation/ventilation

Near-Fatal Asthma

•

Clinical: Raised PaCO₂, severe hypoxaemia, drowsy, exhausted, silent
chest.

•

ABG: PaCO₂ \>6.0 kPa with acidosis.

•

Treatment:

o

Immediate ITU admission

o

Mechanical ventilation

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Severe asthma = PaCO₂ low-normal (still compensating).

•

Life-threatening = PaCO₂ normal/high (tiring, red flag).

•

Near-fatal = PaCO₂ high with acidosis (needs ventilation).

•

IV MgSO₄ = first escalation after nebs +

steroids.

•

IV salbutamol/aminophylline = for refractory or life-threatening
cases.

Mnemonic for escalation: "O²--Nebs--Steroids → Mg → IV
β₂/aminophylline → ITU"

stem: A 75 years-old man with heart Failure. JR 80. BP normal. Treated with Ivabradine. Principal site of action of Ivabradine?
explanation:
Correct Answer

A\) SA node

Key Points from the Scenario

•

75-year-old with heart failure being treated with ivabradine.

•

Heart rate given (80) → ivabradine is a heart rate--lowering agent.

•

Unlike beta-blockers, it acts selectively on the SA node.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (SA Node)

•

Ivabradine blocks the If ("funny") current in the SA node.

•

This current is carried by Na⁺/K⁺ inward mixed current responsible

for spontaneous depolarisation (phase 4)of pacemaker cells.

•

Effect: slows the heart rate without affecting

contractility (inotropy) or AV

conduction.

•

Clinical uses:

o

Symptomatic stable heart failure with reduced EF in sinus rhythm (esp.

if HR \>75 bpm despite beta-blocker or if intolerant).

o

Sometimes in stable angina (when beta-blockers contraindicated).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

SA node

o

Correct: ivabradine inhibits If current → slows pacemaker activity.

AV node

o

Site of action for adenosine, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers.

o

Ivabradine has no effect here.

Bundle of His

o

Drugs like class I antiarrhythmics affect His-Purkinje conduction.

o

Not ivabradine.

Ventricular myocardium

o

Site of action for class I and III antiarrhythmics.

o

Ivabradine doesn't alter contractility.

Atrial myocardium

o

Drugs like class I antiarrhythmics (flecainide)

act here.

o

Not ivabradine.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

Ivabradine = SA node, blocks If current, slows HR without ↓ inotropy.

•

Beta-blockers/CCBs = AV node.

•

Class I/III antiarrhythmics = myocardium/His-Purkinje.

•

Adenosine = AV node.

Antiarrhythmic & Rate-Limiting Drugs: Sites of Action

Drug / Class Principal Site of Action Mechanism / Exam Clue

Ivabradine SA node

Blocks If ("funny") current → slows phase 4

depolarisation → ↓ HR without affecting

contractility/AV conduction

Beta-blockers (e.g., bisoprolol,

propranolol)

AV node (also SA)

↓ sympathetic tone, slow AV conduction → prevent

rapid ventricular response in AF

Non-dihydropyridine CCBs

(verapamil, diltiazem)

AV node

Block L-type Ca²⁺ channels → slow AV nodal

conduction; used in rate control

Adenosine AV node

Transient AV block via A1 receptors →

diagnostic/therapeutic in SVT

Digoxin AV node (indirect vagal effect)

↑ vagal tone → slows AV conduction; useful in AF

with HF

Class I antiarrhythmics (Na⁺

channel blockers: flecainide,

lidocaine, quinidine)

Atrial & ventricular

myocardium, His-Purkinje

system

Class III antiarrhythmics (K⁺

channel blockers: amiodarone,

sotalol)

Atrial & ventricular

myocardium, His-Purkinje

system

Prolong action potential & refractory period

Amiodarone (broad spectrum)

Multi-site (atria, ventricles, AV

node)

Blocks Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺ channels + beta-blockade; very

exam-high yield

(amlodipine, nifedipine)

Loop diuretics / Thiazides Not cardiac conduction

Cause electrolyte disturbances (↓K⁺, ↓Mg²⁺) →

predispose to arrhythmias

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

SA node → Ivabradine.

•

AV node → Adenosine, Beta-blockers, CCBs, Digoxin.

•

Atrial/ventricular myocardium + His-Purkinje → Class I & III

antiarrhythmics.

•

Multi-site → Amiodarone (very exam-friendly).

Mnemonic: "SA → Iva, AV → ABD (Adenosine, Beta-blockers, Digoxin),

Myocardium → Class I/III, Everywhere →

Amiodarone."

Pneumonia history, breathless, cough, rusty sputum

BP normal

Investigations:

Na low, K also low, RFT normal, random sugar high

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Adrenal insufficiency

Hypothyroidism

SIADH

Salt and water depletion

Hyperglycaemia

ANSWERS:

SIADH

Correct Answer

SIADH

Key Points from the Scenario

•

History of pneumonia → classically associated with SIADH (especially
lobar

pneumonia due to Strep. pneumoniae or atypical infections like
Legionella).

•

Findings:

o

Hyponatraemia (Na low)

o

Hypokalaemia (K low) -- can be seen in SIADH (urinary K⁺ loss due to

water handling changes)

o

Normal renal function → excludes renal failure.

o

Random sugar high → likely stress-related hyperglycaemia, but not the

primary diagnosis.

•

BP normal → argues against adrenal insufficiency or volume depletion
(both

cause hypotension).

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (SIADH)

•

SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH secretion):

o

Pneumonia is a classic trigger.

o

Excess ADH → water retention → dilutional hyponatraemia.

o

Serum osmolality low, urine osmolality inappropriately high.

•

Potassium may also be low in SIADH due to renal tubular handling, but
the key

feature is low Na with normal renal function in a

pneumonia setting.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Adrenal insufficiency

o

Would cause hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia + hypotension.

o

Here K is low and BP is normal → not consistent.

Hypothyroidism

o

Can cause hyponatraemia, but no hypothyroid features, and acute

pneumonia is a stronger explanation.

SIADH

o

Correct: pneumonia + low Na with normal RFT + normal BP → SIADH.

Salt and water depletion

o

Would cause hyponatraemia + hypokalaemia, but also hypotension,

high urea/creatinine.

o

Here BP and RFT are normal.

Hyperglycaemia

o

Can cause dilutional hyponatraemia (osmotic shift), but not associated

with pneumonia typically.

o

Also doesn't explain hypokalaemia in this setting.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Pneumonia + hyponatraemia → think SIADH.

•

Addison's = low Na + high K + hypotension.

•

Salt & water depletion = low Na + low K + hypotension +

↑urea/creatinine.

•

Hypothyroidism = chronic, not acute pneumonia setting.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Pneumonia + low Na⁺ = SIADH.

•

Low Na⁺ + high K⁺ + hypotension = Addison's.

•

Low Na⁺ + low K⁺ + hypotension = Salt & water depletion.

•

Low Na⁺ + normal K⁺ + hypothyroid features = Hypothyroidism.

•

Low Na⁺ + high glucose = Pseudohyponatraemia.

Mnemonic: "SALT-H" → SIADH, Addison's, Low thyroid, Thiazides (or GI

stem: A 35-years-old presented with 3 month H/O polydipsia, polyuria. Drinks 4L a day, nocturia 4 times/night. Na 144, U 9, Cr 90, S. Ca 2.7. Glucose normal. Serum Osmol 308. Urine Osmol 120. What is the most likely explanation for this presentation?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Hypercalcaemia

Key Points from the Scenario

•

35-year-old with polyuria + polydipsia + nocturia.

•

Serum Na⁺ = 144 mmol/L (normal--high) → not dilutional hyponatraemia (so

not SIADH or psychogenic polydipsia).

•

Serum Osmolality = 308 mOsm/kg (↑ high) → confirms hyperosmolar state.

•

Urine Osmolality = 120 mOsm/kg (very dilute) → kidneys are failing to

concentrate urine.

•

Serum Ca²⁺ = 2.7 mmol/L (↑ high) → significant hypercalcaemia.

•

Glucose normal → excludes diabetes mellitus.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Hypercalcaemia)

•

Hypercalcaemia impairs renal concentrating ability by antagonising ADH
at

the collecting ducts → produces a picture like nephrogenic diabetes
insipidus.

•

Leads to polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia with dilute urine despite high
plasma

osmolality.

•

This explains why:

o

Serum osmol ↑ (dehydrated).

o

Urine osmol ↓ (kidneys not concentrating).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Hypercalcaemia

o

Correct: elevated Ca²⁺ explains impaired urinary concentrating ability
→

polyuria/polydipsia.

Arginine Vasopressin (ADH) deficiency = Central DI

o

Would cause very similar picture (↑ serum osmol, dilute urine).

o

BUT here we already have hypercalcaemia, a clear reversible cause of

nephrogenic DI.

Exam wants you to pick hypercalcaemia as the etiology.

3\. Diabetes Mellitus

o

Would show high glucose + glycosuria → osmotic diuresis.

o

Here glucose is normal.

4\. Psychogenic Polydipsia

o

Would cause low/normal serum Na⁺ & low serum

osmolality (dilutional).

o

Here serum osmol is high.

5\. SIADH

o

Would cause low Na⁺ + low serum osmol + inappropriately

concentrated urine.

o

Opposite to this case.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Hypercalcaemia → nephrogenic DI picture (polyuria, polydipsia, dilute

urine despite hyperosmolar plasma).

•

Central DI = ADH deficiency.

•

Psychogenic polydipsia = low serum osmol.

•

SIADH = hyponatraemia + concentrated urine.

Osmolality

(osmotic

diuresis)

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Polyuria + hyperglycaemia = Diabetes Mellitus.

•

Polyuria + high serum osmol + dilute urine = Diabetes Insipidus (central

or nephrogenic).

•

Nephrogenic DI causes = Hypercalcaemia, Lithium, Amphotericin.

•

Low serum osmol + dilute urine = Psychogenic polydipsia.

•

SIADH → hyponatraemia + concentrated urine.

Mnemonic: "High--Low--Low--SI"

•

High glucose = DM

•

Low ADH = Central DI

•

Low response = Nephrogenic DI

•

SI = SIADH (low Na + concentrated urine)

Polyuria: Diagnostic Flowchart

Step 1: Check Serum Osmolality

•

↑ High (\>295 mOsm/kg) → think Diabetes Mellitus / Diabetes Insipidus

•

↓ Low (\<275 mOsm/kg) → think Psychogenic Polydipsia / SIADH

Step 2: If Serum Osmol High → Check Urine Osmolality

•

↑ Urine Osmol → Diabetes Mellitus (osmotic diuresis, glycosuria)

•

↓ Urine Osmol (dilute) → Diabetes Insipidus

Step 3: Differentiate Central vs Nephrogenic DI

•

Give Desmopressin (ADH analogue):

o

Urine concentrates (↑ osmolality) → Central DI (ADH deficiency)

o

No response (remains dilute) → Nephrogenic DI (ADH resistance →

causes: hypercalcaemia, lithium, amphotericin B)

Step 4: If Serum Osmol Low → Check Urine Osmolality

•

↓ Urine Osmol (dilute) → Psychogenic Polydipsia

↑ Urine Osmol (concentrated) → SIADH (euvolaemic hyponatraemia, e.g.

pneumonia, SCLC, SSRIs)

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Hypercalcaemia = Nephrogenic DI (polyuria + dilute urine + high serum

osmol).

•

Pneumonia + hyponatraemia = SIADH.

•

Excess water drinking + low serum osmol = Psychogenic Polydipsia.

•

Glucose in urine = Diabetes Mellitus osmotic diuresis.

Mnemonic for Polyuria Work-up: "SO--UO--DD" → Serum Osmol → Urine Osmol
→

Desmopressin test for DI.

stem: A 20-years-old man. Works night shift. H/O beclomethasone nasal spray use. Brother has Adrenoleukodystrophy. Underwent Synacthen test. 9am Cortisol 70. 30 min post Synacthen 575. Why is 9 am Cortisol low?
explanation:
Correct answer

Diurnal rhythm alternated

Key points from the scenario

•

Night-shift worker → circadian rhythm is flipped; cortisol surge occurs

around wake-time, not clock "09:00".

•

Synacthen test: baseline 70 → 575 nmol/L at 30 min = normal adrenal

reserve.

•

Using beclomethasone nasal spray (low systemic absorption) --- unlikely
to

suppress HPA axis meaningfully.

Why the 09:00 cortisol is low?

Cortisol follows a circadian (diurnal) rhythm: highest shortly after
waking, lowest

around midnight. In a night-shift worker, the peak shifts toward the
person's sleep--

wake schedule. Drawing cortisol at 09:00 clock time (which may be his
biological

"night") can therefore show a low value, even when adrenal function is
normal.

The normal Synacthen response (to 575) confirms intact adrenal cortex
and

effectively rules out clinically significant adrenal insufficiency.

Why the other options are less likely

•

Addison's (primary adrenal insufficiency): would show poor/absent

rise after Synacthen; here the rise is robust.

•

Adrenoleukodystrophy: causes primary adrenal failure → blunted

Synacthen response expected.

•

Beclomethasone-induced adrenal suppression: intranasal doses rarely

suppress HPA; if there were significant suppression, response might

be blunted (especially if chronic/high-dose systemic steroids).

•

ACTH deficient (secondary): early/partial secondary AI can have a near-

normal Synacthen, but the stem hands you a far more parsimonious

explanation --- night-shift circadian inversion --- and there's no
pituitary

history; plus, the response is clearly normal.

Key Points:

Low "09:00" cortisol in shift workers can be physiological. A normal
Synacthen rules

out adrenal failure.

A 48 year old with hereditary hemochromatosis presented with joint pain
and fatigue.

Gene for which protein is involved?

⁃ HFE

⁃ Transferrin receptor 2

⁃ Hepcidin

⁃ Haemojuvelin

⁃ Ferroprotein

ANSWERS:

HFE

Correct Answer

HFE

Key Points from the Scenario

•

48-year-old with hereditary haemochromatosis → most common inherited

iron overload disorder.

•

Presents with arthropathy + fatigue (classic early symptoms).

•

The majority of cases are due to mutations in the HFE gene (esp. C282Y,

H63D).

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (HFE gene)

•

HFE protein interacts with the transferrin receptor → regulates hepcidin

production in the liver.

•

Mutation (esp. C282Y homozygous) → impaired hepcidin signalling →

inappropriate intestinal iron absorption → progressive iron overload.

•

Leads to:

o

Liver disease (cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma)

o

Diabetes ("bronze diabetes")

o

Arthropathy (esp. 2nd and 3rd MCP joints)

o

Cardiomyopathy, hypogonadism

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

HFE

o

Correct: classic hereditary haemochromatosis (type 1).

•

Transferrin receptor 2 (TFR2 gene mutation)

o

Causes type 3 haemochromatosis, rarer, later

onset.

•

Hepcidin (HAMP gene mutation)

o

Causes type 2B haemochromatosis (juvenile form), very early onset

and severe.

•

Haemojuvelin (HJV gene mutation)

o

Causes type 2A haemochromatosis (juvenile form).

•

Ferroportin (SLC40A1 gene mutation)

o

Causes type 4 haemochromatosis (autosomal dominant), iron

trapped in macrophages.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Common hereditary haemochromatosis = HFE mutation (C282Y, H63D).

•

Juvenile haemochromatosis = HJV (haemojuvelin) or HAMP (hepcidin).

•

TFR2 = type 3 (rare).

•

Ferroportin = type 4 (dominant).

stem: MLH1 - what is this gene in charge for?
explanation:
Mismatch (DNA mismatch repair gene)

Key Points

•

MLH1 = MutL Homolog 1.

•

Encodes a protein involved in the DNA mismatch repair (MMR) system.

•

Works with other genes (MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) to correct base--base
mismatches

and insertion--deletion loops during DNA replication.

•

Mutations in MLH1 → defective mismatch repair → microsatellite
instability

(MSI) → accumulation of mutations.

Clinical Significance

•

Lynch Syndrome (HNPCC) → commonly due to germline mutations in MLH1

or MSH2.

•

Associated cancers: colorectal, endometrial,

ovarian, gastric, urinary tract.

•

Tumours show microsatellite instability (MSI-high) on testing.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Angiogenesis → driven mainly by VEGF.

•

Apoptosis → controlled by p53, BCL-2 family, caspases.

•

Cell cycle → regulated by cyclins, CDKs, RB gene.

•

Adhesion → linked to E-cadherin (CDH1 gene).

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

MLH1 = DNA mismatch repair gene → Lynch syndrome.

•

Microsatellite instability is the hallmark.

75 yr old female patient with involuntary

throwing movements of left arm and foot,

she has past H/O TIA

Site of lesion?

a\) Caudate nucleus

b\) Globus pallidus

c\) Subthalamic nucleus

d\) Substantia Nigra

e\) Red nucleus

ANSWERS:

Subthalamic nucleus

Correct Answer

c\) Subthalamic nucleus

Key Points from the Scenario

•

75-year-old woman with involuntary, flinging/throwing movements of left

arm & foot.

•

This description = Hemiballismus.

•

Hemiballismus = violent, large-amplitude, proximal limb movements.

•

Classic cause = contralateral lesion in the subthalamic nucleus (often

vascular, e.g. lacunar infarct post-TIA/stroke).

Detailed Explanation (Subthalamic Nucleus Lesion)

•

Subthalamic nucleus is part of the indirect pathway of the basal
ganglia,

normally inhibits movement.

•

Lesion → loss of inhibitory control → excess movement (hemiballismus).

•

Usually unilateral (hemiballismus), contralateral to lesion.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

a\) Caudate nucleus → associated with chorea

(Huntington's disease), not

ballistic movements.

•

b\) Globus pallidus → lesions cause dystonia/rigidity, not
hemiballismus.

•

d\) Substantia nigra → degeneration → Parkinson's disease (bradykinesia,

tremor, rigidity).

•

e\) Red nucleus → lesion leads to tremor, ataxia (midbrain syndromes),
not

hemiballismus.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Hemiballismus = contralateral subthalamic nucleus lesion (classically

vascular).

•

Caudate = chorea.

•

Substantia nigra = Parkinson's.

•

Globus pallidus = dystonia/rigidity.

•

Red nucleus = tremor/ataxia.

stem: 59 yr man came with paracetamol overdose, history of similar overdoses, single man, he calculated the exact dose for suicide . What is associated with an increased risk of completed suicide ?

Patient presenting to Hospital with episode of colicky abdominal pain, 4th admission in the last 1 month. His father passed away 8 years ago due to pancreatic cancer. Previous tests have all been normal Patient is writhing, sweaty, hyperventilating and holding his abdomen allowing only limited examination, mentioned that he wants morphine to help ease the pain otherwise will commit suicide. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct answer

Malingering

Key points from the scenario

•

Recurrent short admissions (4 in 1 month) with colicky abdominal

pain but previous tests all normal.

•

Behaviour on exam: writhing, sweaty, hyperventilating, restricting
exam ---

highly dramatic, disproportionate to objective

findings.

•

Explicit secondary gain: patient demands morphine and says if he does
not

get it he will commit suicide --- a threatened act that appears
contingent on

receiving opioids.

•

Family history (father died of pancreatic cancer) can explain health
concern but

does not fully account for the repeated normal investigations and the
clear

inducement for medication.

Why malingering is the best diagnosis

•

Malingering = intentional production or exaggeration of physical or

psychological symptoms motivated by external incentives (secondary
gain) ---

e.g., obtaining drugs, avoiding work, evading

legal responsibility, or obtaining

shelter/benefits.

•

Here the patient

Repeated presentations with normal investigations → suggests

symptoms may not reflect organic disease.

o

Explicit statement linking desired treatment (morphine) to threat of
self-

harm suggests instrumental/goal-directed behaviour rather than true

suicidal intent.

o

Dramatic, inconsistent presentation (holding abdomen to prevent exam,

hyperventilating on demand) supports voluntary exaggeration.

•

Importantly: malingering is a behavioural/

forensic formulation, not a

psychiatric disorder per se.

Clinical & safety caveat --- always assess for real risk first

•

Even when malingering is suspected, do NOT dismiss the patient. You
must:

Perform an urgent suicide/safety risk assessment. Threats of self-

harm must be taken seriously until proven otherwise. The presence of a

contingent threat increases the likelihood of malingering, but does
not

exclude real intent.

Stabilise medically and check for acute pathology (examine, repeat

targeted investigations if indicated). Some organic disease may show

intermittent signs.

Document carefully objective findings, prior test results, and

inconsistent behaviours.

Manage analgesia and observation safely --- avoid reflexive large

opioid prescriptions if drug-seeking suspected; consider multimodal

analgesia, short, supervised doses, or non-opioid options while you

investigate.

Involve senior clinicians, the pain team, psychiatry liaison, and

safeguarding if necessary.

If after assessment the patient is judged to be at imminent risk, treat

that risk (admit, psychiatric review, remove means). If judged to be

malingering without immediate risk, manage

medically and address

social/psychosocial needs (homelessness, benefits, etc.) that may

underlie the behaviour.

Why the other options are less likely

•

Adjustment disorder --- involves emotional/behavioural symptoms in

response to an identifiable stressor, but not typically repeated
dramatic physical

presentations with clear external incentive (drug seeking) and normal
workups.

Hypochondriasis (Illness anxiety disorder) --- involves excessive worry

about having a serious illness despite reassurance; patients usually
seek

investigations and reassurance rather than producing dramatic acute
pain and

explicit threats tied to medication. The

behaviour here is more clearly

instrumental.

•

Depression --- major depression can cause somatic complaints and genuine

suicidal ideation; however, suicidal statements in depression reflect
pervasive

hopelessness, not a conditional demand ("give me morphine or I will
kill

myself") that suggests external incentive. Still --- screen for
depression because

it can co-occur.

•

Conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder) ---

involves neurological symptoms incompatible with disease (weakness,
non-

epileptic seizures), usually unconscious and not produced for
secondary gain.

The deliberate, goal-directed nature of threats and drug-seeking
argues against

conversion.

Practical next steps (how to manage this patient safely and
professionally)

Immediate safety check: direct, calm suicide risk assessment (intent,
plan,

means, past attempts). If immediate risk → urgent admission and
psychiatric

assessment.

Medical assessment: focused history, examination, review of prior
investigation

results (avoid unnecessary repeat tests), bedside observations,
consider limited

targeted investigations if new red flags arise.

Analgesia plan: start with non-opioid analgesics and multimodal
measures; if

opioid required for acute pain, give supervised,

time-limited, documented

doses and reassess response objectively. Avoid unsupervised take-home
opioid

scripts.

Involve senior staff (ward consultant, liaison psychiatry, pain team)
and discuss

risk of drug-seeking behaviour.

Document objective signs, inconsistencies, prior records, patient
statements

about intent, and the clinical rationale for any prescribing
decisions.

Address underlying needs (social work, housing, mental health support)
---

many patients who malinger have unmet social or psychiatric needs.

If confirmed malingering without immediate suicide risk, manage

boundaries clearly: explain limits of

prescribing, offer appropriate referrals, and

plan follow-up.

Malingering = intentional symptom production for external gain.

•

Always rule out medical/psychiatric emergency first (threats of suicide

require immediate assessment), then consider malingering if behaviour is

clearly instrumental and inconsistent with findings.

stem: 52 yr female with 3 weeks of palpitations. No significant history. BP 110/75. ECG shows AF with ventricular rate 110. She is started on rate control. How long should anticoagulation continue after cardioversion?
explanation:
Correct Answer

4 weeks

Key Points from the Scenario

•

AF duration = 3 weeks → not "acute onset" (\<48h), so anticoagulation
is

needed before cardioversion.

•

She was correctly started on apixaban before cardioversion.

Echo normal, BP stable, no comorbidities.

•

CHA₂DS₂-VASc score:

o

Age \<65 = 0

o

Female sex = +1

o

No HTN, DM, CHF, vascular disease, or stroke/TIA history

→ Total = 1 (from sex only)

•

Guideline principle:

o

Anticoagulation is required ≥3 weeks before and 4 weeks after

cardioversion in almost all patients.

o

After 4 weeks, long-term anticoagulation is continued only if

CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥1 (men) or ≥2 (women).

o

Female sex alone (score = 1) is not considered sufficient to warrant

lifelong anticoagulation.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (4 weeks)

•

This patient's stroke risk is truly low (no other CHA₂DS₂-VASc risk
factors

besides sex).

•

Therefore, after successful cardioversion and 4 weeks of anticoagulation

post-procedure, apixaban can be stopped.

•

Long-term anticoagulation is unnecessary unless AF recurs or new risk
factors

(e.g. HTN, DM, vascular disease) develop.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

2\) 6 months → not guideline-based; no evidence

to continue beyond 4 weeks

if low risk.

•

3\) 1 year → same reason; arbitrary.

•

4\) 3 years → not supported; decision is risk-score based, not
time-based.

•

5\) Lifelong → correct only if CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 (female with other risk
factors,

or male with ≥1). Not correct here since risk is minimal.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

AF \>48h or unknown duration → anticoagulate 3 weeks before + 4 weeks

after cardioversion.

•

Stop anticoagulation if low risk (CHA₂DS₂-VASc 0 in men, 1 in women

from sex only).

•

Continue lifelong if CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥1 (men) or ≥2 (women).

AF: Anticoagulation Rules

Scenario Anticoagulation Requirement Key Exam Clue

AF \< 48 hrs (recent onset)

Start anticoagulation at time of

cardioversion (or immediately after).

No 3-week pre-treatment needed.

AF \> 48 hrs OR unknown duration

≥3 weeks before and ≥4 weeks

after cardioversion.

Even if CHA₂DS₂-VASc = 0 (M) / 1 (F

sex only).

Post-cardioversion -- Low risk

CHA₂DS₂-VASc = 0 (men) OR = 1

(women from sex only)

Anticoagulation can be stopped after

4 weeks if sinus rhythm maintained.

Female sex alone is not an indication

for lifelong anticoagulation.

Post-cardioversion -- Stroke risk

present CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥1 (men) or

≥2 (women)

Lifelong anticoagulation

DOAC preferred (apixaban,

rivaroxaban, dabigatran, endoxaban)

unless contraindicated.

Persistent AF or high recurrence

risk

Lifelong anticoagulation regardless

of rhythm control success.

Especially with structural heart

disease or older age.

High-Yield Exam Pearls

•

3 weeks before + 4 weeks after = golden rule for AF \>48 hrs before

cardioversion.

•

CHA₂DS₂-VASc threshold for lifelong anticoagulation:

o

Men ≥1

o

Women ≥2

•

Female sex alone (score = 1) → NOT an independent indication for
lifelong

anticoagulation.

Mnemonic: "3 Before, 4 After, Score Decides Forever."

AF - Anticoagulation & Cardioversion: High-Yield Flowchart

Step 1: Duration of AF

•

\< 48 hours

⬇

→ Cardioversion immediately (electrical/chemical)

→ Start anticoagulation at time of cardioversion (or immediately after).

48 hours or unknown duration

⬇

→ Anticoagulation for ≥3 weeks before cardioversion

→ Proceed with cardioversion

→ Continue anticoagulation ≥4 weeks after.

Step 2: After Cardioversion → Assess Stroke Risk

Use CHA₂DS₂-VASc:

•

Men = 0

•

Women = 1 (sex only)

⬇

→ Stop anticoagulation after 4 weeks if sinus rhythm maintained.

•

Men ≥1 OR Women ≥2

⬇

→ Continue anticoagulation lifelong (regardless of successful
cardioversion).

Step 3: Choice of Anticoagulant

•

DOAC preferred: Apixaban, Rivaroxaban, Dabigatran, Endoxaban

•

Warfarin: Only if DOAC contraindicated (mechanical valve, severe
mitral

stenosis, severe CKD).

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

"3 before, 4 after, score decides forever."

•

Female sex alone is not an indication for lifelong anticoagulation.

•

Always reassess stroke risk if AF recurs or comorbidities develop.

stem: 36 yr female with disseminated ca cervix on 75mg modified release morphine twice daily. What medicine to be given for breakthrough pain?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Oral morphine solution

Key Points from the Scenario

•

36-year-old female with disseminated cervical cancer → palliative
setting.

•

Already on modified-release morphine 75 mg twice daily (regular

background analgesia).

•

Still has breakthrough pain episodes.

•

Breakthrough pain should be managed with a short-acting opioid of the

same drug (morphine) given as immediate release.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer

•

In opioid prescribing:

o

Modified-release (MR) morphine = baseline pain control.

o

Immediate-release (IR) morphine solution/tablets =

for breakthrough pain.

•

Breakthrough dose = typically 1/6th of total 24-hour opioid dose.

o

Here: 75 mg BD = 150 mg/24 hr total.

o

Breakthrough dose = \~25 mg oral morphine solution PRN.

•

This approach ensures consistency and avoids opioid rotation unless
necessary.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Buprenorphine

o

Partial agonist, not first choice for breakthrough in a patient
already

established on strong opioids.

Fentanyl patch

o

Provides long-acting baseline analgesia, not suitable for rapid

breakthrough pain.

Increase dose of modified-release morphine

Only done if background pain is not controlled, not for breakthrough

episodes.

4\. Oral morphine solution

o

Correct choice: immediate-release morphine for breakthrough pain.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Background cancer pain → controlled with modified-release opioids.

•

Breakthrough pain → controlled with immediate-release opioid of same

type (usually morphine).

•

Dose = \~1/6th of total daily dose, PRN.

stem: 42 y/o man with trisomy 21. Presents with myoclonic epilepsy. What is the treatment of choice?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Sodium Valproate

Key Points from the Scenario

•

42-year-old man with Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome).

•

Presents with myoclonic epilepsy

Myoclonic epilepsy = generalised epilepsy syndrome, not focal.

•

Best treatment: broad-spectrum antiepileptic → Sodium valproate is
first-line

(unless contraindicated).

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer (Sodium Valproate)

•

Valproate is effective against multiple seizure types: myoclonic,
tonic-clonic,

and absence seizures.

•

It enhances GABA-mediated inhibition and stabilises neuronal firing.

•

In myoclonic epilepsy, carbamazepine and phenytoin may actually worsen

seizures (they are narrow-spectrum, more for

focal epilepsies).

•

Ethosuximide is specific for absence seizures, not useful for myoclonus.

•

Valproate is therefore the drug of choice.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Phenytoin → can exacerbate myoclonic seizures.

•

Oxcarbazepine → focal epilepsy drug, may worsen generalised seizures.

•

Ethosuximide → only works in absence epilepsy, not myoclonus.

•

Carbamazepine → can worsen myoclonic and absence seizures.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Myoclonic epilepsy → Sodium valproate first-line.

•

Levetiracetam or lamotrigine can be alternatives if valproate
contraindicated

(e.g., in women of childbearing age).

•

Narrow-spectrum AEDs (carbamazepine, phenytoin, oxcarbazepine) →

avoid in generalised epilepsies (myoclonic, absence).

stem: A 35 year old man presents with progressive memory loss. Recently diagnosed with HIV. MRI shows cerebral atrophy. What is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Correct Answer

HIV encephalopathy

Key Points from the Scenario

•

35-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV.

•

Progressive memory loss = cognitive decline (not acute infection, not
focal

lesion).

•

MRI: cerebral atrophy → global rather than focal process.

•

No acute features (no fever, meningism, focal mass effect).

Detailed Explanation (HIV Encephalopathy)

•

HIV itself can directly cause HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder
(HAND),

including HIV encephalopathy.

•

Pathology: HIV enters the CNS early → infects microglia/macrophages →

chronic inflammation, neuronal injury, cortical and subcortical atrophy

Clinically: progressive memory loss, cognitive decline, psychomotor

slowing, behavioural changes.

•

MRI: generalised cerebral atrophy, often out of proportion to age.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Cerebral toxoplasmosis → Multiple ring-enhancing focal lesions with
seizures,

focal deficits, fever. Not just atrophy.

•

Tuberculous meningitis → Basal meningeal enhancement, hydrocephalus,

cranial neuropathies. Presents with subacute meningitis, not isolated
memory

loss.

•

Cryptococcus meningitis → Raised ICP, headache, confusion, fever. MRI
shows

meningeal enhancement, not pure atrophy.

•

PMLE (Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy, JC virus) →

Demyelinating white matter lesions(non-enhancing, asymmetric), focal

deficits, subacute course. Not pure cerebral atrophy.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

HIV encephalopathy (HAND) → Progressive dementia-like picture + cerebral

atrophy on imaging.

•

Toxo = ring-enhancing lesions.

•

Crypto/TB meningitis = meningeal features.

•

PML = asymmetric white matter lesions, no mass effect.

stem: A 55 year old man is diagnosed with type ll diabetes. He is started on metformin. What is the MOA of metformin?
options: D\) Increase excretion of glucose through renal tubules
E\) Decrease glucose absorption form gut
explanation:
C\) Increase sensitivity of insulin

Key Points from the Scenario

•

55-year-old man with new type 2 diabetes mellitus started on metformin.

•

Question is about mechanism of action (MOA).

•

Metformin is first-line therapy in T2DM unless contraindicated.

Detailed Explanation (MOA of Metformin)

•

Metformin is a biguanide.

•

Its primary action:

o

↓ hepatic gluconeogenesis (main effect).

o

↑ insulin sensitivity in peripheral tissues

(muscle, fat).

o

↑ glucose uptake & utilization.

o

↓ intestinal absorption of glucose (minor effect).

•

Unlike sulfonylureas or insulin, metformin does not stimulate insulin

release → no hypoglycaemia risk when used alone.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

A\) Anti GLP1 uptake → Not metformin; GLP-1 agonists (e.g., liraglutide,

exenatide) work here.

•

B\) Antagonism of GLP1 breakdown → That's DPP-4 inhibitors (e.g.,

sitagliptin).

•

C\) Increase sensitivity of insulin → Correct; metformin improves
insulin

sensitivity & decreases hepatic glucose output.

•

D\) Increase excretion of glucose through renal tubules → That's SGLT2

inhibitors (e.g., dapagliflozin).

•

E\) Decrease glucose absorption from gut → That's mainly α-glucosidase

inhibitors (e.g., acarbose).

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Metformin MOA = ↓ hepatic gluconeogenesis + ↑ insulin sensitivity.

•

First-line T2DM drug unless contraindicated (eGFR \<30, severe CKD, risk
of

lactic acidosis).

•

No hypoglycaemia risk when used alone.

Clinical trial in post renal transplant patients. Trial to see
valganciclovir and valaciclovir

for CMV prevention

Most appropriate significance test?

A\) Chi squared test

B\) Fisher exact test

C\) Mann Whitney test

D\) Logistic regression

E\) T test

ANSWERS:

Chi squared test

Correct Answer

A\) Chi-squared test

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Study design: Clinical trial comparing two drugs (valganciclovir vs
valaciclovir).

•

Outcome: Prevention of CMV infection → a

categorical outcome (Yes/No).

•

Question: Which statistical test is most appropriate to

compare proportions between two independent groups?

Detailed Explanation

•

The Chi-squared test is used to compare categorical variables between

groups, e.g.:

o

Proportion of CMV infection in valganciclovir group vs valaciclovir
group.

•

Assumption: sample size is reasonably large (expected frequency ≥5 in
each

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

B\) Fisher exact test

o

Used instead of Chi-squared when sample sizes are very small (\<5 in a

cell).

o

Not stated here, so exam default = Chi-squared.

•

C\) Mann-Whitney test

o

Non-parametric test for continuous/ordinal data (e.g., median survival

times, pain scores).

o

Not appropriate for categorical outcomes.

•

D\) Logistic regression

o

Used for multivariable analysis of categorical outcomes when adjusting

for confounders.

o

Not required for a simple two-group comparison in an RCT.

•

E\) T test

o

Compares means of continuous variables (parametric data).

o

Not appropriate for binary outcomes.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Binary outcome (event yes/no) between 2 independent groups → Chi-

squared.

•

If n \< 5 in any cell → Fisher exact.

•

Continuous outcome (normal) → t-test.

•

Continuous outcome (non-normal) → Mann-Whitney.

•

Adjusted categorical outcome with multiple covariates → logistic

regression.

Mnemonic: "C-T-M-W-A-K"

•

Chi² / Fisher = Categorical

•

T-test = Two means

•

Mann--Whitney = Medians (non-normal)

•

Wilcoxon = Within-patient

•

ANOVA = Analysis of \>2 means

•

Kruskal--Wallis = Kruskal for non-normal \>2 groups

Which Statistical Test?

Step 1: What is your outcome variable?

•

Categorical (Yes/No, proportions) → go to Step 2A

•

Continuous (numerical, e.g. BP, HbA1c) → go to Step 2B

•

Time-to-event (survival) → Cox regression

Step 2A: Categorical Outcome

•

2 groups, large n (≥5 in each cell) → Chi-squared

•

2 groups, small n (\<5 in a cell) → Fisher exact

•

2 groups → Chi-squared (multiple categories)

Step 2B: Continuous Outcome

👉 Check distribution (normal vs non-normal)

Two independent groups

•

Normal → Unpaired t-test

•

Non-normal → Mann--Whitney U

2 independent groups

•

Normal → ANOVA

•

Non-normal → Kruskal--Wallis

Paired data (before vs after in same patient)

•

Normal → Paired t-test

•

Non-normal → Wilcoxon signed-rank

2 related measurements (repeated measures)

•

Normal → Repeated measures ANOVA

•

Non-normal → Friedman test

Step 3: Looking for association or prediction?

•

Correlation only

o

Normal → Pearson correlation

o

Non-normal → Spearman correlation

•

Prediction / adjust for confounders

o

Binary outcome → Logistic regression

o

Continuous outcome → Linear regression

o

Time-to-event → Cox proportional hazards

Binary outcomes → Chi² or Fisher.

•

Means (normal) → T-test / ANOVA.

•

Medians (non-normal) → Mann--Whitney /

Kruskal--Wallis.

•

Within-patient → Paired t-test / Wilcoxon.

•

Correlation vs Regression → Association vs Prediction.

Mnemonic for quick recall:

"C T M W A K P S L C"

•

Chi² / Fisher = categorical

•

T-test = two means

•

Mann--Whitney = medians

•

Wilcoxon = within-patient

•

ANOVA = \>2 means

•

Kruskal--Wallis = \>2 medians

•

Pearson = correlation (normal)

•

Spearman = correlation (non-normal)

•

Linear = regression (continuous)

•

Cox / Logistic = regression (time-to-event / categorical)

stem: The patient is on statin. Which food to avoid?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Grapefruit

Key Points

•

Statins (especially simvastatin, atorvastatin, lovastatin) are
metabolised by

the CYP3A4 enzyme in the liver.

•

Grapefruit juice contains compounds that inhibit CYP3A4, leading to:

o

↑ Statin blood concentration

o

↑ Risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis

•

Other listed foods (tomato, pomegranate, orange, beetroot) do not
significantly

affect statin metabolism.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Statins + grapefruit juice → dangerous interaction (risk of severe
muscle

toxicity).

•

Safe fruits: orange, pomegranate, apple, tomato, beetroot.

•

Clinical pearl: Always ask about grapefruit juice when reviewing a
patient's

drug history.

stem: A 38 year old, 4 weeks post-renal transplant, is on Prednisolone, Tacrolimus, MMF, Bactrim, Amlodipine, and Statin. Which drug is most nephrotoxic and requires regular level monitoring?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Tacrolimus

Key Points from the Scenario

•

38-year-old, 4 weeks post-transplant.

•

On typical immunosuppressive regimen (Prednisolone, Tacrolimus,

Mycophenolate, plus prophylaxis/adjuncts).

•

K⁺ = 6.2 mmol/L (hyperkalaemia).

•

Need to identify the drug responsible.

Detailed Explanation (Tacrolimus → Hyperkalaemia)

•

Tacrolimus (and ciclosporin) are calcineurin inhibitors.

•

They cause hyperkalaemia by:

Reducing renal potassium excretion (due to

decreased Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase

activity and distal tubular dysfunction).

Acting like a potassium-sparing effect similar to spironolactone.

•

Hyperkalaemia is a well-recognised adverse effect of tacrolimus, often

appearing early post-transplant.

Why Other Drugs Are Less Likely

•

Prednisolone → usually causes hypokalaemia (mineralocorticoid effect),
not

hyperkalaemia.

•

Mycophenolate (MMF) → GI side effects, cytopenias; no effect on K⁺.

•

Bactrim (Co-trimoxazole) → can also cause hyperkalaemia (via
trimethoprim

acting like amiloride), but tacrolimus is the primary culprit here,
especially in

post-transplant hyperkalaemia.

•

Amlodipine → calcium channel blocker, no major effect on potassium.

•

Statin → muscle side effects (myopathy, ↑CK), not hyperkalaemia.

•

Valganciclovir → myelosuppression, renal impairment, but not a direct
K⁺

effect.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

Post-transplant hyperkalaemia = Think Tacrolimus (calcineurin
inhibitor).

•

Bactrim can also contribute → especially if used together.

•

Management: monitor K⁺, adjust immunosuppression, consider stopping

contributory drugs, treat acute hyperkalaemia if severe.

•

•

Nephrotoxicity → Tacrolimus, Cyclosporine (but not Sirolimus).

•

Valganciclovir.

•

•

Increased K⁺,

Nephrotoxicity.

Drug causing erectile dysfunction?

⁃ Statin

⁃ Amlodipine

⁃ Bisoprolol

⁃ Doxazosin

⁃ Ramipril

⁃ Aspirin

ANSWERS:

Bisoprolol

Correct Answer

Bisoprolol

Key Points

•

Erectile dysfunction (ED) is a recognised side effect of β-blockers such
as

bisoprolol, propranolol, atenolol.

•

Mechanism: ↓ sympathetic activity, ↓ penile blood flow, and possible
central

suppression of libido.

•

Among the listed drugs, bisoprolol (a β1-selective blocker) is the most

classically associated.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Statin → Rarely associated; most evidence suggests statins

may improve erectile function due to endothelial benefits.

•

Amlodipine → Calcium channel blockers are

generally not linked to ED.

•

Doxazosin → α-blocker, may cause postural hypotension but

often improves urinary/sexual symptoms in BPH.

•

Ramipril → ACE inhibitors rarely linked to ED; generally neutral or even

beneficial for endothelial function.

Aspirin → Not associated with ED.

•

Most common drug classes causing ED:

o

β-blockers (e.g., bisoprolol, propranolol).

o

Thiazide diuretics (e.g., bendroflumethiazide).

o

SSRIs (antidepressants).

o

Some antipsychotics.

•

Always consider drug history when assessing erectile dysfunction.
