stem: Characteristic of apoptosis death?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Chromatin condensation into vesicles

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Apoptosis (programmed cell death) has distinct morphological features:

Cell shrinkage (not swelling).

o

Chromatin condensation → nucleus fragments into apoptotic bodies.

o

Plasma membrane remains intact → contents packaged into vesicles.

o

No acute inflammation (contrast with necrosis).

o

Phagocytosis of apoptotic bodies by macrophages.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Induction of acute inflammation → Seen in necrosis, not apoptosis.

•

Lysosome rupture → Feature of necrosis, causes autodigestion.

•

Rupture plasma membrane → Necrosis hallmark, not apoptosis.

•

Swelling of organelles → Again, necrosis → "oncosis" (cell swelling).

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Apoptosis = cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, membrane intact, no

inflammation.

•

Necrosis = cell swelling, membrane rupture, lysosomal release,

inflammation.

stem: A patient with H/O RA taking MTX, Sulfasalazine; but no improvement, so planning for TNF inhibitors. Anti-TNF increases the risk of?
explanation:
Correct Answer

A. Serious infection

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Patient with Rheumatoid Arthritis, failed DMARDs (Methotrexate,

Sulfasalazine). Next step = biologic therapy (TNF-α inhibitor:
infliximab,

adalimumab, etanercept).

•

Main risk = serious infections (particularly TB reactivation,
opportunistic

infections, sepsis).

•

Screening for latent TB, hepatitis B & C is mandatory before starting
TNF

inhibitors.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

B. Heart failure → TNF inhibitors can worsen pre-existing HF, but this
is not the

most important risk; infection is the major concern in exams.

•

C. MS → Rare, TNF inhibitors can trigger demyelinating disease, but less

common.

•

D. Malignancy → Slightly increased risk of lymphoma and non-melanoma
skin

cancer, but not the primary exam answer.

•

E. Lupus → Rarely can cause drug-induced lupus (ANA, anti-dsDNA
positive),

but again much less important than infections.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

TNF inhibitors → Serious infection risk (TB reactivation).

•

Checklist before starting: CXR, TB screening (Mantoux/IGRA), Hep B/C

serology.

•

Other associations:

o

Can worsen HF.

o

Can cause demyelination.

o

Rare drug-induced lupus

A 50 year old man with 4 months H/O thirst, polyuria, polydipsia and
weight loss of 6

kg. His father, paternal uncle and brother have T2DM.

Serum creatine Normal

Fasting blood glucose is elevated at 23

Hba1c is markedly elevated at 100

Most appropriate treatment / What should he be

started on?

A. Metformin

B. Gliclazide

C. Insulin

D. Pioglitazone

E. Sitagliptin

ANSWERS:

A. Insulin

Correct Answer

C. Insulin

Key Points from the Scenario

•

50 y/o man with classic osmotic symptoms → thirst, polyuria, polydipsia,

weight loss.

•

Marked hyperglycaemia:

o

Fasting glucose = 23 mmol/L (very high).

o

HbA1c = 100 mmol/mol (extremely uncontrolled).

•

Weight loss → suggests catabolic state (insulin deficiency).

•

Even though strong family history suggests T2DM, this presentation with

symptomatic hyperglycaemia + catabolism requires immediate insulin.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

A. Metformin → First-line in stable T2DM, but contraindicated in
symptomatic

severe hyperglycaemia with weight loss.

B. Gliclazide → Sulfonylurea stimulates insulin secretion but inadequate
for this

severity.

•

D. Pioglitazone → Insulin sensitiser, slow onset, inappropriate in acute
severe

hyperglycaemia.

•

E. Sitagliptin → DPP-4 inhibitor, mild glucose-lowering effect, not
suitable

here.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Symptomatic hyperglycaemia + weight loss + HbA1c \> 85 or glucose \> 20

→ Insulin therapy.

•

Once stable, some can be transitioned to oral agents if truly T2DM.

•

Always rule out T1DM / LADA if presentation atypical.

stem: A middle-aged female with pain in spine, pelvis, thigh, shoulder, proximal muscle weakness. Ca = 2.1, Phosphate = low, ALP = increased What would be most appropriate next investigation?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Serum 25-OH (Vitamin D)

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Middle-aged female with bone pain (spine, pelvis, thigh, shoulder) +

proximal muscle weakness → points to osteomalacia.

•

Biochemistry pattern:

o

Calcium = low-normal (2.1)

o

Phosphate = low

o

ALP = raised

→ Classic for osteomalacia / vitamin D deficiency.

•

Best initial investigation: Serum 25-hydroxy vitamin D (25-OH) = storage

form, best marker of body vitamin D status.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Bence Jones Protein → Myeloma, would show hypercalcaemia, lytic lesions,

not low phosphate + high ALP.

•

Bone Density Screen (DEXA) → Detects osteoporosis, but not diagnostic
for

osteomalacia.

•

PTH → May be elevated secondarily (secondary hyperparathyroidism), but

primary test is 25-OH vitamin D.

•

Thyroid function → Thyroid disease can affect bone, but biochemistry
here

points to vitamin D deficiency.

•

Electrophoresis → For myeloma, not relevant here.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Osteomalacia labs:

o

Low/normal Ca

o

Low phosphate

o

High ALP

o

Low vitamin D

•

Best first investigation = Serum 25-OH vitamin D.

stem: A 55 year old post-inferior MI PCI. 2 hours post-procedure: ECG shows PVCs and ventricular bigeminy. HR 80/min, BP 120/80 mmHg. What is the management?
explanation:
Correct Answer

E. No intervention

Key Points from the Scenario

•

55 y/o man, Inferior MI, PCI done.

•

2 hrs later: PVCs + Ventricular bigeminy.

•

Pulse 80/min, BP stable (120/80).

•

Isolated PVCs / ventricular bigeminy after MI are very common and
usually

benign if:

o

Patient is haemodynamically stable.

o

No sustained VT/VF.

o

No ongoing chest pain or instability.

•

Best management = observation only, no anti-arrhythmics.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

A. Amiodarone → Used in sustained VT or haemodynamically unstable

ventricular arrhythmias. Not needed for benign PVCs.

•

B. Flecainide → Class Ic agents contraindicated post-MI (increase
mortality).

•

C. Lidocaine Previously used for post-MI PVCs but no mortality benefit →
not

recommended anymore unless malignant arrhythmia.

•

D. Magnesium sulphate → Used in torsades de pointes, not isolated PVCs.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Post-MI PVCs = usually benign → no treatment if

stable.

•

Treat only if:

Haemodynamic compromise, sustained VT, or VF → then use

amiodarone / DC cardioversion depending on stability.

•

Never use flecainide post-MI (pro-arrhythmic).

Post-MI Arrhythmias: Stepwise Management

Ventricular Ectopics (PVCs / Bigeminy / Couplets)

•

Very common after MI

•

If haemodynamically stable → No intervention (just monitor)

•

Do not use prophylactic anti-arrhythmics

(flecainide, lidocaine)

Ventricular Tachycardia (VT)

•

Sustained & stable → IV Amiodarone

•

Unstable (hypotension, syncope, shock, chest pain) → Immediate DC

cardioversion

Ventricular Fibrillation (VF)

•

Immediate defibrillation (unsynchronised shock)

•

Follow ACLS protocol

Bradyarrhythmias / AV Block (esp. Inferior MI)

•

Asymptomatic, stable → Monitor (often transient)

•

Symptomatic / unstable → Atropine IV → Temporary pacing if persistent

•

Anterior MI with new high-grade block → High risk, pacing often
required

Atrial Arrhythmias (AF, Atrial Flutter)

•

Common in first 24--48h post-MI

•

Rate control (β-blocker / amiodarone) if persistent

•

Consider anticoagulation (CHA₂DS₂-VASc)

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

PVCs post-MI = benign → NO treatment.

•

Amiodarone = stable VT.

•

DC shock = unstable VT / VF.

•

Atropine = symptomatic bradycardia.

•

Never give flecainide post-MI.

A 30 year old with low back and buttock pain for 3 months, heel pain &

1 episode of red eye 1 year back.

Morning stiffness of 1 hr improves by afternoon.

What would be the most suitable test for diagnosis?

ESR

Lumbar x ray

MRI spine

ANSWERS:

MRI spine

Correct Answer

MRI spine

Key Points from the Scenario

•

30 y/o, chronic low back + buttock pain, heel pain (enthesitis), past
red

eye (uveitis), morning stiffness improving with activity → classic for
Axial

Spondyloarthritis (Ankylosing Spondylitis type picture).

•

Best test for early diagnosis:

o

MRI sacroiliac joints / spine → detects active sacroiliitis (bone marrow

oedema, inflammation).

o

X-ray lumbar spine → useful but only detects late changes (sacroiliitis,

bamboo spine).

o

ESR → supportive marker of inflammation, but not diagnostic.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

ESR → Non-specific; may be normal in axial spondyloarthritis.

Lumbar X-ray → Detects structural damage, but disease often present for
years

before radiographic changes appear.

•

MRI spine → Picks up early inflammation → gold standard for early
diagnosis.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Suspected axial spondyloarthritis (young, inflammatory back pain,

enthesitis, uveitis):

o

Best test = MRI SI joints / spine.

o

X-ray only if long-standing disease.

o

HLA-B27 and ESR/CRP support but not diagnostic.

stem: A middle aged man with extremely painful defecation, hard stool, and bright red blood after defecation. Initial step in management?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Lactulose

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Middle-aged man, painful defecation, hard stool, bright red blood →
likely

anal fissure secondary to chronic constipation

First step = soften stools to reduce trauma and pain → stool softeners
(e.g.,

lactulose, docusate).

•

This reduces straining, allows fissure healing.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Ispaghula husk (bulk-forming) → Can worsen pain initially by increasing

stool bulk when fissure is present.

•

Sodium Picosulfate (stimulant) → Increases peristalsis, may worsen anal

pain/fissure.

•

Senna (stimulant) → Same as above; not first choice in fissure-related

constipation.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Anal fissure management (initial):

o

Stool softeners (lactulose, docusate).

o

High-fibre diet + hydration.

o

Topical GTN or diltiazem if persistent.

•

Avoid stimulant/bulk-forming agents initially in fissure pain.

•

70 y/o man, prior TB history, nasal lesion for 1 year, ala nasi

destroyed/eroded.

•

Lupus vulgaris = cutaneous tuberculosis → classically causes chronic,
slowly

progressive, destructive lesions on the face (esp. ala of nose, cheeks,
ears).

•

•

Trigeminal neuralgia and tropical references irrelevant here.

•

Cutaneous sarcoidosis → Causes plaques/nodules, not destructive nasal
ala

erosion.

•

Vasculitis with polyangiitis (GPA) → Causes septal destruction (saddle
nose),

•

BCC → Ulcer with pearly rolled edges, usually on sun-exposed skin, not
TB-

•

Tropical trigeminal neuralgia → Not relevant, doesn't cause skin lesion.

Lupus vulgaris = most common cutaneous TB, often on face/nose, slow

destruction of ala nasi.

stem: A 33 y/o with fever, weight loss, palpitations successfully treated for thyroid storm with Hydrocortisone, B Blocker, Propylthiouracil. What\'s the function of hydrocortisone?
options: Reduced conversion from T4 to T3
explanation:
Correct Answer

Reduced conversion from T4 to T3

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Thyroid storm is life-threatening thyrotoxicosis.

•

Standard therapy includes:

o

β-blocker (symptom control).

o

Thionamide (PTU, carbimazole) → inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis

(PTU also blocks peripheral conversion of T4 → T3).

o

Iodine (after Thionamide) → blocks release of

thyroid hormone.

o

Glucocorticoids (Hydrocortisone or Dexamethasone):

▪

Reduce T4 → T3 peripheral conversion.

▪

Provide adrenal support (relative adrenal insufficiency common in

thyroid storm).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Decreased thioperoxides → That's the mechanism of thionamides (PTU,

carbimazole), not steroids.

•

Fix cortisol deficiency → Hydrocortisone can support adrenal reserve,
but the

high-yield mechanism in thyroid storm is inhibition of peripheral T4 →
T3

conversion.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Hydrocortisone in thyroid storm:

↓ T4 → T3 conversion.

Covers possible adrenal insufficiency.

•

Propylthiouracil: blocks thyroid peroxidase + T4 → T3.

•

β-blocker: symptom control + ↓ T4 → T3 conversion (propranolol).

•

Iodine: blocks hormone release (but only after thionamides).

A 54 y/o/m with Hep C

Anti-HCV positive, but viral load undetectable

Reasons for PCR being negative?

Carrier state

Previous infections

ANSWERS:

Previous infections

Correct Answer

Previous infection

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Anti-HCV positive → means the patient has been exposed to hepatitis C
virus

at some point.

•

PCR (viral load) undetectable → no active viral replication.

•

This combination most commonly indicates:

o

Cleared past infection (either spontaneously or after treatment).

•

Important distinction:

o

HCV does not have a "carrier state" like HBV.

o

If viral load is undetectable, the patient does not have ongoing
infection.

Why Other Option Is Less Likely

•

Carrier state → Term applies to Hepatitis B (HBsAg positive, no
symptoms).

o

Hepatitis C is either active (RNA positive) or resolved (RNA negative,

antibodies positive)

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Anti-HCV +, RNA -- → Past resolved infection.

•

Anti-HCV +, RNA + → Active infection.

•

Anti-HCV --, RNA + → Early infection (window period).

stem: Elderly man comes with thoracic back pain. He has T8 collapse. Investigations included deranged kidney functions, elevated total protein, hypercalcaemia What investigations should be done?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Serum electrophoresis

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Elderly man with T8 vertebral collapse + back pain.

•

Biochemistry: deranged kidney function, hypercalcaemia, elevated total

protein.

•

This is the classic triad of Multiple Myeloma:

o

CRAB criteria = Calcium ↑, Renal impairment, Anaemia, Bone lesions.

o

Elevated total protein → due to monoclonal immunoglobulin.

•

Best diagnostic test = Serum protein electrophoresis (detects
M-protein /

paraprotein).

Often combined with urine electrophoresis (Bence-Jones protein) and
serum

free light chains.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

PSA → For prostate cancer (can metastasise to bone) but doesn't explain
high

protein + renal failure.

•

ESR → Will be raised in myeloma but nonspecific; not diagnostic.

•

Serum ACE → Marker for sarcoidosis; irrelevant here.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Elderly + back pain + CRAB + high protein → Multiple Myeloma → Serum

electrophoresis.

•

Always think "vertebral collapse + hypercalcaemia + renal failure =

Myeloma until proven otherwise."

stem: Urine culture is persistent negative with fever and weight loss for 6 months. Leukocyte 3+ Diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer

TB (Genitourinary tuberculosis)

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Persistent sterile pyuria (Leukocyte 3+, but culture negative) + chronic

symptoms (fever, weight loss, 6 months) → classic red flag for renal /

urinary tuberculosis.

•

Sterile pyuria = WBCs in urine but no growth on standard culture →
strongly

suggests TB, chlamydia, or interstitial nephritis.

•

Here, systemic features (fever, weight loss, chronic course) point to
TB.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Chlamydia → Can cause sterile pyuria, but usually presents as urethritis

(younger sexually active patients), not prolonged fever + weight loss.

•

Schistosomiasis → Causes terminal haematuria, bladder wall
calcification, and

is geographical (Africa/Middle East exposure). Not sterile pyuria with
systemic

symptoms.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Sterile pyuria + systemic illness → think renal TB.

•

Confirm with urine AFB culture / PCR (3 early morning samples).

•

Other sterile pyuria causes: Chlamydia, interstitial nephritis, renal
stones,

partially treated UTI.

stem: Green sputum pneumonia and lady want pregnancy safe drug. Treatments?
explanation:
Correct Answer

A. Amoxicillin

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Green sputum + pneumonia → typical bacterial pneumonia (likely

Streptococcus pneumoniae or H. influenzae).

•

Patient wants a pregnancy-safe antibiotic.

Antibiotic safety in pregnancy:

•

Amoxicillin (β-lactam) → Safe in pregnancy

•

Clarithromycin (macrolide) → Generally avoided in 1st trimester, may be

considered later if penicillin allergy.

•

Moxifloxacin (fluoroquinolone) → Contraindicated in pregnancy (cartilage

damage).

•

Doxycycline (tetracycline) → Contraindicated in pregnancy (teeth

discoloration, bone growth problems).

Why Amoxicillin is Best Here

•

Covers common typical pneumonia pathogens.

•

Safe in all trimesters of pregnancy.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

First-line in pregnancy pneumonia → Amoxicillin.

•

If penicillin-allergic → Erythromycin (preferred macrolide), not

clarithromycin early pregnancy.

•

Avoid fluoroquinolones & tetracyclines

Reslizumab MOA?

Ab against IL-5

IgE

Macrophage

Natural Killer cells

Mast cells

ANSWERS:

Ab against IL-5

Correct Answer

Ab against IL-5

Key Points

•

Reslizumab = humanized monoclonal antibody.

•

MOA: Binds to interleukin-5 (IL-5) → prevents it from activating
eosinophils.

•

Used in severe eosinophilic asthma (not responsive to standard
inhalers).

•

Reduces airway inflammation, asthma exacerbations, and steroid

dependence.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

IgE → That's Omalizumab.

•

Macrophage → No direct effect.

•

Natural Killer cells → No role.

•

Mast cells → Cromolyn sodium stabilises mast cells, not Reslizumab.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Reslizumab / Mepolizumab / Benralizumab → IL-5 inhibitors
(eosinophilic

asthma).

•

Omalizumab → anti-IgE.

•

Dupilumab → anti-IL-4/IL-13.

MOA OF IMATINIB?

Inhibits C-kit

BRAF

mTOR inhibitors

TNF inhibitors

ANSWERS:

Inhibits C-kit

Correct Answer

Inhibits C-kit

Key Points

•

Imatinib = tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI).

•

Targets BCR-ABL fusion protein (Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22)) in
CML.

•

Also inhibits C-kit (mutated in GIST -- gastrointestinal stromal
tumors) and

PDGFR.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

BRAF → Targeted by Vemurafenib / Dabrafenib (melanoma).

•

mTOR inhibitors → Examples: Sirolimus, Everolimus, Temsirolimus.

•

TNF inhibitors → Examples: Infliximab, Adalimumab, Etanercept (RA,
IBD).

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Imatinib → inhibits BCR-ABL + C-kit + PDGFR.

•

CML & GIST = hallmark indications.

A patient went to the United States & presented with small erythema 1
week which

increase in size.

Dx?

Erythema chronicum migrans

Erythema multiforme

Erythema ab igne

ANSWERS:

Erythema chronicum migrans

Correct Answer

Erythema chronicum migrans

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Travel to USA → Lyme disease endemic area (Borrelia burgdorferi).

•

Rash: small erythema that expands in size over days to weeks → classic

description of erythema chronicum migrans.

•

Pathognomonic early skin lesion of Lyme disease.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Erythema multiforme → Target / "bull's-eye" lesions, often after HSV or

Mycoplasma, but they are multiple, fixed, not expanding annular lesion.

•

Erythema ab igne → Reticulated, hyperpigmented rash due to chronic heat

exposure (e.g., hot water bottle, heater).

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Erythema chronicum migrans = expanding annular rash with central

clearing → diagnostic for early Lyme disease

A 23 y/o presents with weakness, increase frequency on laugh and black
out.

Dx?

A. Cataplexy

B.Absent Seizure

C. Non Epileptic attack

D. Periodic paralysis

E. Reflex Epilepsy

ANSWERS:

A. Cataplexy

Correct Answer

A. Cataplexy

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Trigger: Symptoms occur on laughing → strong emotional trigger.

•

Weakness + blackout-like episode = sudden loss of muscle tone without
loss

of consciousness.

•

This is cataplexy, which is a hallmark feature of narcolepsy.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Absence seizure → Brief staring spells, no emotional trigger, usually in
children.

•

Non-epileptic attack → Psychogenic, not specifically triggered by
laughter,

often prolonged.

•

Periodic paralysis → Episodic weakness linked to K⁺ disturbances, not

laughter.

•

Reflex epilepsy → Triggered by specific stimuli (flashing lights,
reading, music),

but not laughter.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Cataplexy = emotionally triggered sudden loss of muscle tone (laughing,

anger, surprise).

•

Strongly associated with narcolepsy (with sleep paralysis & hypnagogic

hallucinations).

stem: A patient presents with a velvety, hyperpigmented lesion on the neck. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Influenza scenario Antivirals of choice?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Oseltamivir

Key Points from the Scenario

Influenza → caused by influenza A & B viruses.

•

First-line antiviral: Neuraminidase inhibitors (Oseltamivir, Zanamivir).

•

Effective if started within 48 hours of symptom onset.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Tenofovir → Nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) → used in
HIV &

Hepatitis B, not influenza.

•

Ribavirin → Broad-spectrum antiviral, sometimes used in RSV and
Hepatitis C

(with interferon), not standard for influenza.

•

Influenza → Oseltamivir / Zanamivir.

•

High-risk or hospitalized patients benefit the most.

stem: Drug causing pancreatitis?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Azathioprine

Key Points

•

Drug-induced pancreatitis is a well-known complication of Azathioprine
(and

6-mercaptopurine).

•

It usually develops within weeks of starting therapy, even at standard
doses.

•

Mechanism thought to be idiosyncratic hypersensitivity, not
dose-related.

Why Not Mesalazine?

•

Mesalazine (5-ASA) can rarely cause interstitial nephritis, but
pancreatitis is

far more strongly linked with Azathioprine.

•

In IBD, if pancreatitis occurs, azathioprine/6-MP are the usual
culprits.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Drugs causing pancreatitis:

o

Azathioprine

o

Didanosine

o

Valproate

o

Furosemide, Thiazides

o

Steroids

o

Alcohol

stem: A 70 y/o with right eye blindness & headache IgG Low. IgA low. IgM high. Electrophoresis showed monoclonal band of IgM. Dx?
explanation:
Correct Answer

A. Waldenström macroglobulinaemia

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Age: Elderly (70 y/o).

•

Symptoms: Right eye blindness + headache → suggestive of hyperviscosity

syndrome.

•

Immunoglobulin pattern:

o

IgM very high (monoclonal spike on electrophoresis).

o

Low IgG and IgA (suppressed by monoclonal expansion).

•

This exactly fits Waldenström macroglobulinaemia (a lymphoplasmacytic

lymphoma producing excess IgM).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Cryoglobulinemia → IgM can precipitate, but diagnosis requires

cryoprecipitate + vasculitis features (purpura, Raynaud's, GN). Here,
clear

monoclonal IgM band points to Waldenström.

•

Heavy chain deposition disease → Rare, produces only heavy chains, not

intact IgM monoclonal spikes.

•

MGUS → Usually asymptomatic, no end-organ damage, and IgM not this high

with hyperviscosity.

•

Multiple Myeloma (MM) → Usually IgG / IgA monoclonal spike, lytic bone

lesions, renal failure --- not isolated IgM

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Waldenström macroglobulinaemia = IgM monoclonal gammopathy +

hyperviscosity syndrome (visual disturbance, headache, bleeding,

neuropathy).

•

Treatment often requires plasmapheresis for hyperviscosity + systemic

therapy.

stem: A patient presented with a H/O renal transplant with multiple warty lesions on the scalp & firearm. What is the next step?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Skin biopsy

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Renal transplant → patient is immunosuppressed (↑ risk of skin
cancers).

•

Multiple warty lesions on scalp & forearm → could be viral warts (HPV)
but

in immunosuppression always suspect premalignant / malignant

transformation (esp. squamous cell carcinoma).

•

Skin biopsy is essential to establish whether these are benign warts
or

Why Not HPV PCR?

•

HPV PCR → would only detect viral DNA, not helpful in determining
malignant

transformation.

•

In transplant patients, the priority is ruling out skin cancer → biopsy
gives

histology, which is diagnostic.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Transplant patients → 65--100x ↑ risk of SCC of skin due to long-term

immunosuppression.

•

Any suspicious / new / multiple warty or keratotic lesions → biopsy
first.

stem: Smoking Cessation counselling + shows the high cessation rate of more than 6 months?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Varenicline

Key Points

•

Varenicline = partial agonist at α4β2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor

It reduces cravings and withdrawal symptoms, while also blocking
nicotine's

rewarding effects.

•

Clinical trials consistently show highest quit rates \>6 months compared
to

NRT or bupropion.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Nicotine inhaler / patch → effective, but lower long-term cessation
rates

compared to varenicline.

•

Hypnotherapy → evidence is weak and inconsistent.

•

Bupropion → effective (dopamine & noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor), but
quit

rates are lower than varenicline, and it carries a seizure risk.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Best pharmacological aid for smoking cessation = Varenicline (highest

long-term abstinence).

•

NRT (patch, inhaler, gum) = useful, especially if contraindication to

varenicline/bupropion.

•

Bupropion = alternative, but less effective.

stem: A 76 y/o woman was driving 36h ago. Experienced sever vertigo, right nystagmus with fast horizontal oscillation towards right. Past pointing on examination. CTB showed Mild small Vessel disease. What is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Cerebellum Stroke

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Acute severe vertigo lasting \>24h (36h here) → rules out BPPV (seconds-

minutes, positional).

•

Nystagmus: horizontal, direction-fixed to the

right → consistent with central

lesion.

•

Past pointing (dysmetria) → classic cerebellar sign, not seen in
isolated

labyrinthitis or Ménière's.

•

CT brain showed only mild small vessel disease → early cerebellar
infarcts may

be missed on CT; MRI is more sensitive.

•

Sudden severe vertigo + cerebellar signs = posterior circulation stroke.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

BPPV → transient (\<1 min), positional, no persistent vertigo or past
pointing.

•

Labyrinthitis → post-viral, vertigo with hearing loss, no cerebellar
signs.

•

Ménière's → recurrent episodes (minutes--hours), associated with
tinnitus +

fluctuating SNHL. Not continuous severe vertigo with past pointing.

•

Top of Basilar → causes brainstem/cortical symptoms (visual changes,

confusion, quadriparesis), not isolated vertigo with cerebellar signs.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Vertigo + cerebellar signs (past pointing, dysmetria, ataxia) =
cerebellar

stroke until proven otherwise.

•

CT may miss posterior circulation strokes → MRI brain with DWI is
diagnostic.

stem: Alcoholic patient who stopped drinking for a couple of days presented with delirium & confusion. Delirium tremors management apart from thiamine?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Chlordiazepoxide

Key Points from the Scenario

Alcohol withdrawal (delirium tremens): occurs 2--3 days after stopping

alcohol.

•

Features: confusion, agitation, tremor, hallucinations, autonomic

overactivity.

•

Mainstay of treatment = benzodiazepines.

•

Chlordiazepoxide (long-acting benzodiazepine) is the drug of choice in
most

cases.

•

Lorazepam may be preferred if liver disease / elderly / risk of
oversedation.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Chlorpromazine → antipsychotic, can lower seizure threshold, dangerous
in

alcohol withdrawal.

•

Disulfiram → used for relapse prevention, not in acute withdrawal.

•

Lorazepam → correct drug class (benzodiazepine), but not first-line
unless

concern about liver impairment.

•

Risperidone → antipsychotic, not used in withdrawal.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

DT management:

o

Thiamine before glucose (prevent Wernicke's).

o

Benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide / diazepam).

o

IV fluids, electrolyte correction, monitor vitals.

stem: 22 year old man with pleuritic chest pain. CXR normal. Chest tenderness on examination. Next step?
options: Discharge — musculoskeletal chest pain, no further investigations
explanation:
Correct Answer

Discharge without further investigations

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Young man (22 y/o), pleuritic chest pain, normal CXR, and tender chest

wall on examination.

•

The presence of localized tenderness strongly suggests musculoskeletal

chest pain (costochondritis / pleuritic strain) rather than PE, ACS, or

pneumonia.

•

No red flags, stable vitals, and normal CXR → safe to discharge with

reassurance + analgesia.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

D-dimer → indicated only if there is clinical suspicion of PE with

low/intermediate probability (Wells score). Here, musculoskeletal cause
is

obvious.

•

CTPA → high radiation/contrast risk, reserved for suspected PE after
positive D-

dimer or high Wells score.

•

ECHO → used if suspecting cardiac cause (pericarditis, tamponade, RV
strain

from PE), not in chest wall tenderness.

•

V/Q Scan → alternative to CTPA in pregnancy or renal impairment, not
needed

here.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Chest wall tenderness + normal CXR = musculoskeletal cause → no further

investigation.

•

Always use Wells score + clinical context before ordering D-dimer or
CTPA for

PE.

A 70 y/o woman presents with 2 weeks H/O stiffness in morning over
shoulder, hip.

ESR is elevated. CK is not elevated. ANA is raised. RF is raised.

Dx?

⁃ PMR

⁃ Fibromyalgia

⁃ Polymyositis

⁃ RA

⁃ SLE

ANSWERS:

PMR

Correct Answer

PMR (Polymyalgia Rheumatica)

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Age: 70 years old → PMR typically affects \>50 yrs.

•

Symptoms: Morning stiffness of shoulders + hips → classic for PMR.

•

Labs:

o

ESR elevated (inflammatory).

o

CK normal (rules out polymyositis).

o

ANA / RF raised: can sometimes be weakly positive in elderly; not

specific here.

•

Fibromyalgia: pain and fatigue but normal ESR/CRP.

•

RA: more distal joint (MCP, PIP), with synovitis.

•

SLE: multi-system features, rash, cytopenias.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Fibromyalgia → normal ESR/CRP, no objective inflammation.

stem: A 35 y/o presents with depression, memory loss 2/12. MOCA 25/30. On Examination showed mild ataxia. Small amplitude jerking. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Wilson's disease

Key Points from the Scenario

Age: Young adult (35 y/o).

•

Neuropsychiatric features: Depression, memory loss → common early

presentations of Wilson's.

•

Examination: Mild ataxia + small amplitude jerks (tremor/asterixis-like

movements) → classic neurological signs in Wilson's.

•

MOCA 25/30 → mild cognitive impairment, fits

with subcortical

neurodegeneration.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

PMLE → Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, occurs in

immunocompromised, causes rapid cognitive decline and focal neurology,
not

jerking/ataxia in otherwise healthy 35 y/o.

•

MS → Typically relapsing--remitting, with optic neuritis, sensory or
motor

deficits. Not progressive jerks + psychiatric + hepatic features (often

accompany Wilson's).

•

Huntington → Presents with chorea, behavioral changes, and dementia,

usually with strong family history (autosomal dominant). Not small
amplitude

jerks/ataxia.

•

Adrenoleukodystrophy → X-linked, presents earlier
(childhood/adolescence)

with adrenal insufficiency + myelopathy.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Wilson's disease = Hepatic + Neurological + Psychiatric.

•

Investigations: ↓ ceruloplasmin, ↑ urinary copper, Kayser--Fleischer
rings.

stem: Seizure. Presents with Pain over Left rhumb. Loss of awareness. Dystonic posturing of arms and legs. General convulsion. Site of Epileptic centre?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Temporal lobe

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Loss of awareness → strongly suggests focal impaired-awareness seizure

(previously complex partial), most common in temporal lobe epilepsy.

•

Aura: pain over left thumb → sensory aura, can occur with temporal
seizures

due to limbic and sensory network involvement.

•

Dystonic posturing of limbs → automatisms and motor involvement are

characteristic of temporal seizures.

•

Secondary generalization → focal onset (temporal) evolving into
generalized

tonic--clonic.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Frontal → seizures are usually brief, nocturnal, bizarre motor
posturing,

often without aura.

•

Brainstem → would cause syncope-like collapse, cranial nerve/autonomic
signs,

not classic seizure progression.

•

Parietal → focal sensory seizures (tingling, numbness, pain), but loss
of

awareness + automatisms point more to temporal than pure parietal.

•

Thalamus → generalized epileptiform activity (absence seizures), not
focal with

aura.

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Temporal lobe epilepsy = aura (déjà vu, sensory/autonomic), impaired

awareness, automatisms, dystonic posturing, secondary generalization.

Torsade De pointes. Management?

⁃ MgSO4

⁃ Adenosine

⁃ Amiodarone

⁃ Flecainide

⁃ Lidocaine

ANSWERS:

MgSO4

Correct Answer

MgSO₄ (Magnesium sulfate)

Key Points

•

Torsades de pointes = polymorphic ventricular

tachycardia associated with

prolonged QT interval.

•

First-line acute management = IV magnesium sulfate, even if magnesium
level

is normal.

•

Mechanism: stabilizes myocardial membrane, reduces early after

depolarisations that trigger torsades.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Adenosine → used for SVT (AVNRT), not ventricular arrhythmias.

•

Amiodarone → can actually worsen QT prolongation → contraindicated in

torsades.

•

Flecainide → Class IC antiarrhythmic, can worsen

arrhythmias in structural

heart disease.

•

Lidocaine → used in ventricular arrhythmias post-MI, but not torsades
(QT

prolongation arrhythmia).

MRCP Syndrome Clinical Pearls:

•

Torsades = give MgSO₄ first.

•

If unstable → DC cardioversion.

•

Long-term: stop offending drugs, correct K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, consider pacing
if

recurrent.
